title: The Monetary 101 Rulebook
subtitle: Money and value from the ground up, written to be passed down, so each generation keeps what the last one learned and does not repeat what it forgot.
intro: Most people use money every day and never learn how it works. Nobody teaches it at home, school teaches a little arithmetic, and the news speaks a language of rates, yields and deficits that seems designed to keep outsiders out. This guide is meant to open that locked room, slowly and clearly, one idea at a time.

It starts at the very bottom, with what money actually is, and climbs step by step: gold coins and the gold standard, the wars that broke it, the 1944 system that crowned the dollar, the 1971 night that cut the dollar loose from gold, the oil money that followed, and the way banks create most of our money today with a few keystrokes. Then it turns to the questions that matter for your life: why debt never seems to go away, why prices move in long seasons, why empires and their currencies fall, why the ruler we measure prices with keeps stretching, and how a new player with no inheritance can get onto the board.

It is written like a rulebook passed from one generation to the next. Each chapter ends with rules. The book ends with a full rulebook and a list of the mistakes each generation made, from Rome to the 2020s, so that their intelligence and their errors are both preserved.

The guide honors the ideas of the person who commissioned it, an owner who wrote a newsletter series about money called Ledger Age, and quotes their questions in their own words. Where their intuition is right, the guide says so and builds on it. Where it needs correcting, the guide corrects it gently and shows the evidence.

History and economics here are kept to what is well established. Where scholars disagree, the guide says so. Current numbers, as of October 22, 2026, come from this project's own research files. This is general education about how money works, not financial advice for any person's situation.
howToRead: Read the chapters in order the first time. Each one builds on the one before, and later chapters assume the earlier ideas.
Do not rush. Each chapter has one big picture to hold in your head, usually in a box marked Picture this. If you remember the picture, you will remember the idea.
Try every self-check before reading the answer. Saying an answer out loud, even a wrong one, is how the idea moves from the page into your head.
Watch for the insider boxes. They point to things most people never notice, often hiding in plain sight in official numbers.
Myth and reality boxes are not there to mock anyone. Most myths are half true, and the reality usually keeps the true half.
Use the glossary whenever a word feels slippery. Every technical term in the guide is defined there in plain words.
Read the rulebook at the end once a year. Rules that feel obvious now will feel very different in a crisis.
This is education, not advice. Test any rule against your own situation, and get a second opinion before big decisions.

chapters.title: What money really is
chapters.kicker: Money is not a thing you hold. It is a promise that a whole society agrees to keep track of.

blocks.text: Ask ten people what a dollar is and most will say paper, or numbers in an app, or the stuff you buy things with. All three answers describe what money looks like. None of them says what money is. This chapter fixes that, because every later chapter stands on it.

Here is the short version. Money is a record of who owes what to whom, written in a unit that everyone agrees to use. The paper, the coin and the app are only the places where the record is kept. Once you see money as a record, a lot of confusing things in finance suddenly make sense.
The story you were taught

Most textbooks tell a neat story. Long ago people bartered. A baker wanted shoes, but the shoemaker did not want bread. Trade was clumsy. So people picked one handy good, like silver or shells, that everyone would accept. That good became money. Later, banks and credit were built on top of it.

Adam Smith told a version of this story in The Wealth of Nations in 1776, with his butcher, brewer and baker. A century later the economist William Stanley Jevons gave the problem a name: the double coincidence of wants. Barter only works when each side happens to want what the other has, at the same moment.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Imagine a school lunchroom with no money. You have a sandwich and want an apple. The kid with the apple wants cookies, not your sandwich. You would need to find a third kid, trade the sandwich for cookies, then trade cookies for the apple. Lunch would be over before you ate. That is the barter problem, and it is real. The question is whether people ever actually lived that way.
What the records actually show

When historians and anthropologists went looking for whole societies that ran on barter, they did not find them. What they found, again and again, was credit. People kept running tabs with neighbors. They settled up later, often at harvest time, and they measured the debts in a shared unit.

items: Mesopotamia, about 5,000 years ago: temple and palace clerks kept clay tablet accounts. Debts and prices were written in weights of silver and measures of barley. Most farmers never touched the silver. The silver was a unit for keeping score, not a coin in every pocket.

Medieval England: the royal treasury, the Exchequer, recorded tax debts on notched hazel sticks called tallies. The stick was split in two, and each side kept half. Tallies were used from the 1100s until 1826. When officials burned the old sticks in 1834, the fire got out of control and burned down most of the Palace of Westminster.

The island of Yap in the Pacific: people used huge carved stone discs called rai. Big stones rarely moved. Everyone simply remembered who owned which stone. One stone was said to lie at the bottom of the sea after a canoe accident, and it still counted as wealth, because the community agreed it existed.

blocks.text: Each case says the same thing. The core of money was the shared memory of who owed what. The physical object, when there was one, was a token of that memory.
No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money.

blocks.myth: Money was invented to fix barter, and credit came later.
blocks.reality: In most of the record, credit and accounts came first, and coins came much later. Barter does show up, but mostly between strangers who do not trust each other, or when a money system breaks down, as in prisoner of war camps where cigarettes became currency, or in Russia in the 1990s. Some economists still defend the barter story as a useful thought experiment rather than history. That is a fair use, as long as nobody mistakes it for what happened.

blocks.caption: The textbook path runs from barter to coins to credit. The historical record mostly runs the other way: credit and accounts first, coins later, and barter mainly when trust or money breaks down.

blocks.text: The three jobs of money
Whatever form it takes, money does three jobs. Learn these three words well. They come back in every chapter.

rows: The thing people hand over to settle a trade
Nobody will accept it, so you cannot spend it
A way to carry buying power from today into the future
Savings you will use next year
Prices rise fast, so the same money buys less later
The measuring stick for prices, wages and debts
Your rent is written as $1,500 a month
The unit keeps changing size, so contracts become guesses

blocks.caption: Money does three jobs at once: it settles trades, it carries value through time, and it measures everything. A good money does all three. Many things do one or two.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of money as the scoreboard in a game that the whole country plays at once. The scoreboard does not make the points. Players make the points by working, building and trading. The scoreboard just records them so everyone can see the score, compare it and carry it into the next round. If someone can secretly change the scoreboard, the game stops being fair. Hold on to this picture. We will use it again and again.

The quietest job is the most powerful one. Whoever controls the unit of account controls the terms of every contract written in it. Your wage, your mortgage, your rent and the national debt are all written in dollars. If the dollar shrinks in value, every one of those contracts changes meaning without anyone signing anything new. That is why governments defend the unit of account harder than anything else.
Trust is the hidden ingredient

A dollar bill is worth something to you because you expect the next person to take it. That person accepts it because they expect the person after them to take it. Money is a long chain of expectations. Break the chain and money becomes paper again.

Governments help hold the chain together in a simple way. They demand taxes in their own money. If you must pay the tax office in dollars, you need dollars, so dollars have value. The German economist Georg Friedrich Knapp built a whole theory on this idea in 1905. Economists still argue about how much taxes matter compared with habit, law and the sheer convenience of using what everyone else uses. Most agree that all of these help.
It exists not by nature but by law.
blocks.by: Aristotle, on money, Nicomachean Ethics, about 350 BC

blocks.text: When trust breaks, it breaks fast. Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008 saw prices doubling in days. People stopped using the local money and fled to foreign currency, to gold, or to goods. The paper did not change. The promise behind it did.
The owner's four phases, read carefully

The author of this project, writing a newsletter called Ledger Age, described four phases of value. Phase 1 was physical (gold and silver, stored labor plus scarcity). Phase 2 was symbolic (paper as a promise of gold). Phase 3 was political (fiat money, a promise of control). Phase 4 is digital (credit, crypto and ledgers, a promise of data). In the owner's words, Phase 4 did not end the game, it removed the referee.

This is a strong way to see the big arc, and the rulebook keeps it. Two gentle corrections make it sharper. First, the phases overlap rather than follow one another, because credit and ledgers are the oldest layer, not the newest. Mesopotamian clerks were running Phase 4 style ledgers in clay. Second, the referee has not left. Central banks, courts and regulators still referee the game, as later chapters show. What digital ledgers changed is speed and reach: the scoreboard now updates in seconds, everywhere at once.

blocks.q: Your friend says money is valuable because it is backed by gold. Using this chapter, what is a better answer?
blocks.a: Money is valuable because people trust that others will accept it, because the government demands it for taxes, and because debts and prices are written in it. Gold backing is one way to build that trust, but the dollar has not been backed by gold since 1971.

blocks.q: Which of the three jobs of money is failing when prices rise 50% in a year?
blocks.a: Mainly the store of value, because savings lose buying power. The unit of account also suffers, because prices and contracts become hard to compare over time.

rules: Money is a record of who owes what. Ask who made the promise and who keeps the ledger.
Check all three jobs. A money that fails one of them will eventually fail the others.

connects.how: Gold coins were one way to make the promise trustworthy, and the next chapter shows what that cost.
Today most money is born as a bank ledger entry, which is the modern version of the clay tablet.
The unit of account job returns as the yardstick problem.

chapters.title: Commodity money and the gold standard
chapters.kicker: Tying money to a metal makes it honest. It also makes it stiff, and stiff money breaks people who owe it.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 showed that money is a promise. The oldest way to make a promise believable is to tie it to something hard to fake. For thousands of years that something was metal, mostly silver and gold. This chapter is about what metal money did well and why it was finally abandoned.
Coins: a promise you can bite

The first known coins appeared around 600 BC in Lydia, in what is now Turkey. They were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, stamped with a mark. The stamp was the important part. It said: the king guarantees the weight and purity of this metal. You no longer had to weigh and test every piece.
Metal money has a built-in brake. Nobody can create gold by decree. It must be mined, which takes work and time. That scarcity is why people trusted it as a store of value.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of a coin as a sealed jar of honey with a royal label. The label saves you from opening and tasting every jar. But the label is only as good as the person who sealed the jar. If the king starts adding water and keeping the label, the jars still look the same while the honey gets thinner.
Debasement: watering the honey

Rulers who needed more money than they had found a trick. Melt the coins, mix in cheaper metal, strike more coins with the same face. This is called debasement. It is the ancient version of printing money.

Rome is the classic case. The silver denarius, introduced around 211 BC, was nearly pure silver for a long time. Under Nero in the 60s AD its weight and silver content were trimmed. Through the crisis years of the 200s AD, emperors who had to pay armies kept cutting. By the 260s and 270s the denarius and its successor coins held only a few percent of silver, a thin coating over bronze. Prices soared. In 301 AD the emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for over a thousand goods, on pain of death. It failed. Goods vanished from markets, and the edict was quietly ignored.

Debasement and modern inflation share a pattern. The first people to spend the new coins, the emperor and his soldiers, got full value. By the time the extra coins spread through the economy, prices had risen, and the last people to receive them lost. Chapter 17 calls this the Cantillon effect.
Gresham's law: bad money drives out good

When two coins have the same face value but one contains more real metal, people spend the bad one and hoard the good one. The good coins disappear from circulation. This is Gresham's law, named after Sir Thomas Gresham, a financial agent to Queen Elizabeth I. The idea is older. Nicole Oresme in the 1300s and Nicolaus Copernicus in 1526 described it. The name was attached in 1858.

You can see Gresham's law today. In the United States, silver dimes and quarters minted before 1965 vanished from pockets within a few years after cheaper copper-nickel coins arrived. People kept the silver ones.
The classical gold standard, about 1870 to 1914

Britain drifted onto a gold standard after 1717, when Isaac Newton, as Master of the Mint, set a gold price for the guinea that left silver undervalued. Britain made it law in 1821. After 1871 the newly united Germany switched to gold, and much of the world followed. The United States stopped coining silver dollars in 1873, resumed paying gold for its paper in 1879 and made gold the legal standard in 1900.

The rule was simple. Each currency was defined as a fixed weight of gold. Banks and central banks promised to swap paper notes for gold at that fixed rate. Because every major currency was tied to gold, they were also tied to each other. A pound was worth about $4.86 for decades.

blocks.caption: Under the gold standard, paper notes are claims on gold at a fixed price. Because each currency is fixed to gold, exchange rates between currencies are fixed too.

blocks.text: The system had an automatic balancing idea, first described by the Scottish philosopher David Hume in 1752. A country that imported too much paid in gold. Gold flowed out. Its money supply shrank. Prices and wages fell. Its goods got cheaper, exports recovered, and gold flowed back. Elegant on paper. Painful in real life, because falling wages and prices mean layoffs and bankruptcies.

cols: What the gold standard did well
rows: Could not expand money when the economy needed it
Made exchange rates predictable for trade and lending
Forced painful deflation on countries losing gold
Limited a government's ability to print its way out of trouble
Tied money growth to mining luck, not to the needs of the economy
Turned every banking panic into a scramble for scarce gold

blocks.text: Why fixed money hurt debtors

Here is a key idea of the whole rulebook. When money is fixed but the economy grows, there is more stuff to buy with the same amount of money. Prices fall. That is deflation. Falling prices sound pleasant until you owe money.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: A farmer in Kansas borrows $1,000 in 1880 when wheat sells for $1 a bushel. The debt is worth 1,000 bushels. By 1894 wheat sells for about half that. The farmer still owes $1,000, but now it takes about 2,000 bushels to pay. The farmer works twice as hard to pay the same debt. The lender, without lifting a finger, is repaid in money that buys twice as much wheat.

That is roughly what happened. From 1873 to 1896, prices in the United States and Britain drifted downward for more than two decades. The economy grew, but farmers and other debtors were crushed by rising real debts. The American Populist movement demanded more money, especially free coinage of silver, to stop the squeeze.
You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.
blocks.by: William Jennings Bryan, Democratic National Convention, 1896

blocks.text: Bryan lost the 1896 election. Then something unplanned ended the deflation anyway: new gold. Huge finds in South Africa and the Klondike, plus a new chemical process for extracting gold from ore, expanded the world's gold supply. From 1897 prices rose gently, and farm distress eased. The money supply had been set by miners, not by anyone's plan.

blocks.myth: Gold-backed money is always fair to everyone.
blocks.reality: Gold money is fair to lenders and savers in a growing economy, because it gains buying power. It is harsh on borrowers, because their debts get heavier as prices fall. Whether a money is fair depends on whether you owe it or own it, and on which way prices are moving. Chapter 9 calls these the seasons of money.

blocks.text: The owner's project tested a popular claim that the world's gold, times ten, equals the world's debt. The ratio is real today, about 12 times, but in the past it wandered from about 35 times in 1971 to about 53 times in 2000 and 23 times in 2010. A real mechanism would show a stable ratio. This one moves mainly with the gold price, so it is a coincidence, not a rule. No legal link between gold and dollar credit has existed since 1971.

blocks.q: Why did falling prices from 1873 to 1896 hurt farmers more than bankers?
blocks.a: Farmers owed fixed dollar debts while the prices they received for crops fell, so each dollar of debt took more crops to repay. Bankers were owed those fixed dollars, which bought more as prices fell.

blocks.q: What is Gresham's law, in one sentence?
blocks.a: When two moneys have the same face value but different real value, people spend the worse one and hoard the better one, so the bad money circulates and the good money disappears.

rules: Hard money protects savers and squeezes borrowers. Know which one you are.
When rulers need money they cannot raise honestly, they water down the currency. Watch for it.
When two moneys circulate side by side, the one people hoard is the one they trust.

connects.how: Metal was one answer to the trust problem from Chapter 1.
War broke the gold standard, and Bretton Woods tried to rebuild it around the dollar.
The 1873 to 1896 squeeze is the first deflationary season in the seasons chapter.

chapters.title: War, Bretton Woods and the dollar's crown
chapters.kicker: Two world wars moved the world's gold to America, and in 1944 the dollar became the hub of every other currency.

blocks.text: The gold standard of Chapter 2 worked best in peacetime. War is the most expensive thing a nation ever does, and governments at war will always choose victory over a fixed gold price. This chapter follows how the wars broke the old system and how a new one was designed in a New Hampshire hotel.
The wars break the rules

When the First World War began in 1914, the warring countries suspended gold convertibility. They printed money and borrowed heavily to pay for the fighting. Between 1914 and 1920 prices roughly doubled in the United States, rose even more in Britain, and rose far more again in Germany.

After the war, countries tried to rebuild the gold standard. Britain returned to gold in 1925 at its old prewar rate of about $4.86, a decision made by Winston Churchill as Chancellor. The pound was now overvalued, so British exports were too expensive, and the country suffered high unemployment. John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a pamphlet called The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill.
In truth, the gold standard is already a barbarous relic.
blocks.by: John Maynard Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform, 1923

blocks.text: When the Great Depression struck after 1929, the gold standard spread the damage. Countries losing gold had to raise interest rates and shrink their money supply in the middle of a collapse. Britain left gold in 1931. The United States effectively left domestic gold in 1933, when President Roosevelt ordered citizens to hand in most gold coins and bullion, then raised the official price from $20.67 to $35 an ounce in 1934. Research by economists Barry Eichengreen and Jeffrey Sachs found that countries that left gold earlier generally recovered sooner.
Why America ended up with the gold

Through the 1930s and the Second World War, gold poured into the United States. Europeans sent gold to safety. Allied countries paid for American weapons, food and fuel. By the late 1940s the US government held roughly two thirds of all the gold owned by the world's governments. America also had the only large industrial economy that had not been bombed.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Imagine a long poker night where every player keeps losing chips to one player who also owns the casino's only working kitchen. By dawn that player holds most of the chips. When the others want to start a new game, they have little choice but to use that player's chips as the house standard. That is roughly the position of the United States in 1944.
Bretton Woods, July 1944

In July 1944, delegates from 44 Allied nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Two men shaped the talks. Keynes, for Britain, proposed a new international clearing unit called bancor, which would push both deficit and surplus countries to adjust. Harry Dexter White, for the US Treasury, proposed a system built around the dollar. The country with the gold won the argument.

items: The US dollar was fixed to gold at $35 an ounce. Foreign central banks, not private citizens, could swap dollars for gold at that price.
Other currencies were pegged to the dollar at fixed rates, allowed to move only about 1% either way. Pegs could be changed only for a serious imbalance.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was created to lend to countries with short-term payment problems, so they would not need to devalue or crash their economies.
The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, now part of the World Bank, was created to finance rebuilding and development.

blocks.caption: Bretton Woods, 1944: other currencies pegged to the dollar, and the dollar pegged to gold at $35 an ounce. The dollar became the hub, gold the anchor.

blocks.text: This made the dollar the hub of a wheel. To defend its peg, a country needed a stock of dollars to buy its own currency when it fell. So central banks around the world began to hold dollars, and soon US Treasury bills, as their main reserves. The reserve role of the dollar, which still shapes your mortgage rate today, was born in this design.
A system that worked, then strained

For about two decades the system delivered. Europe and Japan rebuilt quickly. The United States gave about $13 billion in Marshall Plan aid from 1948 to 1952, which put dollars into European hands. Trade grew fast, and inflation was mostly moderate. Many economists call the 1950s and 1960s a golden age of growth.
But the system had a crack in its foundation, spotted early by the Belgian economist Robert Triffin. He laid it out in testimony to Congress in 1959 and in a book in 1960.
The Triffin dilemma

The world needed more and more dollars as trade grew. The only way foreigners could get more dollars was for the United States to send more dollars abroad than it took back, by buying imports, investing overseas, or spending on military bases and aid. Year after year, that piled up dollars in foreign hands.

But each of those dollars was a claim on American gold at $35. As foreign dollar holdings grew, they eventually exceeded the gold the US held. By the early 1960s that line had been crossed. If everyone asked for gold at once, the US could not pay.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: A popular bakery issues tickets, each good for one loaf. Tickets are so trusted that the whole town uses them as money. The town grows and wants more tickets. The bakery keeps printing them, but it cannot bake much more bread. Every new ticket makes the town happier today and the bakery's promise weaker tomorrow. If the bakery stops printing, the town's trade seizes up. If it keeps printing, one day a crowd shows up wanting bread for every ticket. That is the Triffin dilemma.
The dilemma is this. If the US stops supplying dollars, the world economy runs short of money. If it keeps supplying them, confidence in the gold link erodes. Either way, the system is on a timer.

Governments tried patches. In 1961 the US and European central banks formed the London Gold Pool to hold the market price of gold at $35. France, under President Charles de Gaulle, began swapping its dollars for gold and publicly called for a return to a pure gold standard in 1965. The French finance minister Valery Giscard d'Estaing complained of America's exorbitant privilege: the ability to pay for things with its own currency that others must earn. The Gold Pool collapsed in 1968. The countdown to 1971, the subject of Chapter 5, had begun.

blocks.myth: The US took the world's gold by force or trickery.
blocks.reality: Most of it arrived through ordinary channels: European capital fleeing war and instability in the 1930s, and Allied payments for American goods during the war. The result gave the US enormous leverage at Bretton Woods, but it was mostly the product of the US being the safe, unbombed workshop of the world, not a heist.

blocks.text: The United States still holds about 261.5 million ounces of gold, about 8,134 tonnes, according to the Treasury's own records for September 2026. It books that gold at $42.22 an ounce, a price set by law in 1973, so the official value is about $11 billion. At market prices it is worth about $1.08 trillion. The gap is a fossil of the Bretton Woods era still sitting in today's government accounts.

blocks.q: Under Bretton Woods, could an American citizen walk into a bank and swap dollars for gold?
blocks.a: No. Only foreign central banks and governments could convert dollars to gold at $35. American citizens were not even allowed to own most gold bullion from 1933 until 1975.

blocks.q: State the Triffin dilemma in two sentences.
blocks.a: The world needed a growing supply of dollars, which the US could only provide by running deficits with the rest of the world. But the more dollars piled up abroad, the less believable the promise to convert them into gold became.

rules: Wars break money rules. Expect any fixed money promise to be suspended in a great crisis.
The country that holds the reserves usually writes the rules of the next system.
A promise that must grow to keep the world supplied will eventually outgrow what backs it.

connects.how: Bretton Woods was a softened gold standard, with the dollar standing between gold and everyone else.
The habit of holding dollars and Treasuries that began here is the engine of the next chapter.
The Triffin dilemma ended in the 1971 closing of the gold window.

chapters.title: How the world gets its dollars
chapters.kicker: Americans buy more than they sell, foreigners earn the difference in dollars, and those dollars come home as loans to the US government.

blocks.text: Chapter 3 ended with a puzzle. The world wants dollars. How does it get them? The answer is the most important circuit in modern finance. Once you see it, you will notice it in the price of your phone, your mortgage rate and the news about sanctions.
The loop in one breath

items: Americans, as a group, buy more goods and services from the world than they sell to it. This is the trade or current account deficit.
Paying for those imports sends dollars abroad. Foreign exporters now hold dollars.
The exporters, or their central banks, need somewhere safe to keep those dollars that also pays interest.
The deepest, safest place is US government debt: Treasury bills, notes and bonds. So they buy Treasuries, or other US assets such as stocks, companies and property.
The dollars flow back into the US financial system, help fund the US government's deficit and keep US interest rates lower than they would otherwise be.
With rates lower and goods cheap, Americans keep buying, and the loop turns again.

blocks.caption: The recycling loop: the US deficit sends dollars abroad, foreigners earn them by exporting, and they send them back by buying US Treasuries and other US assets.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Imagine a family that shops every day at a neighbor's store and pays with IOUs. The neighbor does not cash the IOUs. Instead, the neighbor deposits them right back with the family, which pays a little interest. The family keeps shopping, the neighbor keeps selling, and the neighbor's pile of IOUs keeps growing. Both are happy as long as the neighbor trusts the family's IOUs. That is the dollar loop, in kitchen terms.
Level one: you, the individual
The loop touches your life in at least two ways, even if you never think about foreign exchange.

items: Cheap imports. Because foreign makers are happy to be paid in dollars and to hold them, Americans can buy goods from all over the world at low prices. The project's time price data show a television costs roughly 99.5% fewer hours of work than in 1993. Clothing, electronics and toys are cheap partly because of this loop.

Lower borrowing costs. When foreigners buy Treasuries, they push up their prices and push down their yields. Since mortgage rates and car loan rates follow Treasury yields, American borrowers benefit. One well known study by Francis and Veronica Warnock estimated that foreign buying lowered the 10-year Treasury yield by close to a percentage point in the mid-2000s.

blocks.text: The flip side for individuals is quieter. If your job was in a factory that competed with imports, the same loop may have cost you that job. More on that below.
Level two: businesses

Picture a Japanese carmaker selling cars in Ohio. It is paid in dollars. It needs yen to pay its workers at home, so it can sell the dollars. But if every exporter sold dollars at once, the yen would soar and Japanese goods would become expensive. So a lot of those dollars stay as dollars. Some are invested by the company in US factories and assets. Some are swapped with Japanese banks and pension funds, who buy Treasuries. Some are absorbed by Japan's central bank and Ministry of Finance as reserves.

The same pattern holds for a Chinese electronics maker, a German machine builder or a Gulf oil company. The project's files show a modern version: Gulf sovereign funds now recycle their dollars into US artificial intelligence infrastructure as owners, for example a roughly $40 billion deal by MGX and BlackRock for a large data center company.

When a foreign company sells you a product, it often ends up lending you, the US taxpayer, the money you paid it. Your dollars leave as payment and come back as a loan to the US government. The trade deficit and the foreign holding of US debt are two sides of the same coin.
Level three: governments

At the top level, foreign governments hold dollars as reserves: a rainy day fund to defend their currency, pay for imports in a crisis and reassure investors. As of August 2026, Japan held about $1,068 billion of US Treasuries, the United Kingdom about $1,010 billion and China about $591 billion, according to US Treasury data gathered by this project. Foreign official accounts held about $2.55 trillion in custody at the New York Fed in mid-October 2026.

For the US government the loop brings two powers. First, it can borrow cheaply and at enormous scale, because the world needs its debt as a safe asset. Second, because most international payments pass through dollar accounts at US banks, the US can cut a country or a company out of the system. In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, Western governments froze roughly $300 billion of Russia's central bank reserves. That showed every government on earth that dollar reserves come with a political condition.

blocks.caption: The same dollar loop seen at three levels: individuals get cheap imports and lower loan rates, businesses earn dollars and invest them in US assets, governments hold Treasuries as reserves while the US gains borrowing and sanctions power.

blocks.text: Why the model works

rows: The US has about $31.8 trillion of marketable Treasury debt. You can buy or sell billions in minutes without moving the price much. No other safe asset is that large or liquid.
Courts enforce contracts and property rights fairly reliably, even for foreigners. Investors fear arbitrary seizure less in the US than in most alternatives.
Oil, commodities, loans and trade are already priced in dollars, so everyone needs dollars, so more things get priced in dollars. Like a language, the more people use it, the harder it is to switch.
Money can enter and leave the US freely. China, the largest rival economy, still restricts this, which limits the yuan as a reserve.
The US security umbrella over allies such as Japan, South Korea, Germany and the Gulf states gives them extra reasons to hold dollars.

blocks.text: What the model costs

items: Hollowed industry. A strong dollar makes US exports expensive and imports cheap. Economists David Autor, David Dorn, Gordon Hanson and coauthors estimated that the surge of Chinese imports in the 2000s cost around a million US manufacturing jobs, and perhaps two million jobs in all. Whole towns felt it.
Persistent deficits. The US has run trade deficits almost every year since the mid-1970s. Foreign claims on the US keep growing.

Borrowing becomes easy, maybe too easy. With the world eager to buy its debt, Washington faces little market pressure to balance its budget, until the price of borrowing finally rises, as Chapter 17 shows it now has.

Dependence on foreign buyers. If foreign governments slow their buying or sell, US rates rise. In 2026 Japan's Treasury holdings fell about $171 billion from February to August as it defended the yen, and long-term US yields rose.

blocks.myth: The trade deficit shows the US is losing.
blocks.reality: Economists disagree about what drives the deficit. One view, associated with Ben Bernanke's 2005 'global saving glut' speech, says foreigners save too much and push their savings into the US, so the deficit is partly caused abroad. Another view, argued by Michael Pettis and others, says surplus countries hold down their own consumption, which forces deficits onto the US. A third view blames low US saving. All three agree the deficit is the mirror image of foreign capital flowing into the US, and that this brings benefits and real costs to different groups of Americans.

blocks.text: The dollar is our currency, but your problem.
blocks.by: John Connally, US Treasury Secretary, to European finance ministers, 1971

blocks.text: Connally said this as the Bretton Woods system cracked. It captures the deal in one line. Because the world holds dollars, American decisions about the dollar land on everyone else. The next chapter shows the moment that line was spoken in earnest.

blocks.q: If foreign central banks stopped buying US Treasuries, what would likely happen to US mortgage rates, and why?
blocks.a: They would likely rise. Fewer buyers for Treasuries means lower prices and higher yields, and mortgage rates follow Treasury yields.

blocks.q: Name one benefit and one cost of the dollar loop for an ordinary American.
blocks.a: Benefit: cheaper imported goods and lower loan rates. Cost: jobs lost in industries that compete with imports, and a government that can borrow without much discipline.

rules: Every trade deficit is also a capital inflow. Follow the dollars both ways.
Cheap imports and cheap loans are paid for somewhere, often by the workers whose industries shrink.
Reserves held in someone else's currency come with someone else's conditions.

connects.how: The habit of holding dollar reserves began with the Bretton Woods design.
After 1971, oil money joined this loop and became the petrodollar.
Stablecoins are becoming a new channel in this same recycling loop.
Sanctions power through dollar plumbing is one of the eye-openers.

chapters.title: 1971, oil and the petrodollar
chapters.kicker: On a Sunday night in August 1971, the last thread between the dollar and gold was cut, and oil quietly took gold's place in the loop.

blocks.text: Chapter 3 ended with a timer. Foreign governments held more dollars than the US held gold. Chapter 4 showed why the world kept piling up dollars anyway. This chapter is the moment the timer ran out, and the surprising thing that happened next.
The run on the bakery

Through the late 1960s, US spending rose on two fronts at once: the Vietnam War abroad and the Great Society programs at home. Inflation crept up. Foreign central banks looked at their growing piles of dollars and at America's shrinking pile of gold, and started asking for gold. In the summer of 1971 Britain reportedly asked to protect a large part of its dollar holdings. The bakery in our Chapter 3 picture had a crowd at the door.
August 15, 1971

President Richard Nixon gathered his advisers at Camp David and then went on national television on a Sunday evening. He announced a package: a 90-day freeze on wages and prices, a 10% surcharge on imports, and the step that changed the world's money.
I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets.

Temporarily turned out to mean permanently. Foreign central banks could no longer swap dollars for gold. The dollar was now backed by nothing physical at all. It was backed by the US government's promise, the US economy, and the fact that the whole world already used it.

blocks.caption: Before August 1971: dollar convertible to gold at $35 for foreign central banks. After: the gold window closed, and by 1973 the major currencies floated against each other.

blocks.text: From fixed to floating

Governments tried to patch the system. In December 1971 the Smithsonian Agreement devalued the dollar to $38 an ounce of gold and reset other pegs. In February 1973 the official price was raised again to $42.22. By March 1973 the major currencies gave up pegs and began to float, meaning their prices against each other were set every day by markets.

That $42.22 is still in the US government's books today. The Treasury values its 261.5 million ounces of gold at exactly $42.2222 an ounce, as of September 2026, while the market price is around $4,100. A number set in a 1973 emergency is still sitting in the national accounts.

blocks.reality: It does not. No one can swap dollars for gold at a fixed price, and no law ties the amount of dollars to the amount of gold. The US government still owns a lot of gold, but it is an asset on the shelf, not a backing for the currency. What anchors the dollar today is the taxing power of the US government, the size of the US economy, and the Federal Reserve's management of interest rates.

blocks.text: Oil enters the loop

Two years after Nixon's announcement, in October 1973, Arab members of OPEC (the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) imposed an oil embargo on the United States and other countries over the Arab Israeli war. Oil prices roughly quadrupled within months, from about $3 a barrel to about $12. Suddenly, oil exporters were collecting a flood of dollars.

Where would that flood go? In 1974, US Treasury Secretary William Simon traveled to Saudi Arabia. The two governments reached an understanding. Saudi Arabia would invest a large share of its oil earnings in US Treasury securities, through special arrangements that kept its purchases out of the normal auctions and kept its holdings secret. In return the US offered military cooperation and security. Oil continued to be priced in dollars, which was already the norm.

The details stayed hidden for decades. In 2016 a Freedom of Information Act request by Bloomberg News uncovered the arrangement, and the US Treasury published Saudi Arabia's Treasury holdings for the first time.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Recall the neighbor who deposits the family's IOUs right back with the family. Now give that neighbor a gas station that every driver in the world must use, with prices quoted in the family's IOUs. The neighbor's pile of IOUs grows enormously, and the neighbor parks it with the family. That is the petrodollar: oil priced in dollars, and the oil money recycled into US government debt.
What the petrodollar was, and what it was not

items: It was three things: oil invoiced in dollars, Gulf oil surpluses recycled into Treasuries and US banks, and a security relationship between Washington and Riyadh.
It was not the dollar's backing. The dollar would remain the world's main currency without it, because of the pillars in Chapter 4.
It is not suddenly over. A viral story claimed a 50-year petrodollar pact expired in June 2024. This project's research found that claim false. There was no such dated pact to expire.

It is fading slowly. Saudi Arabia now holds about $141 billion of Treasuries, about 1.5% of foreign holdings, and in 2026 Gulf states borrowed in markets more than they recycled. Electric vehicles are slowly eating into oil demand.

blocks.text: In the 1970s, banks also recycled petrodollars by lending them to developing countries in Latin America. When US interest rates jumped in the early 1980s, those borrowers could not pay. Mexico defaulted in 1982 and much of Latin America lost a decade. Recycled money always lands somewhere, and the landing is not always soft.
The Great Inflation

With no gold anchor and two oil shocks (1973 and again after the Iranian revolution in 1979), US inflation climbed through the decade. Consumer price inflation peaked near 14.8% in early 1980. Savers who held cash or long-term bonds watched their wealth melt. Workers saw wages chase prices in a race they kept losing. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans, by contrast, quietly gained, because they repaid in cheaper dollars.

Policymakers tried wage and price controls, which caused shortages, and stop and go policy, which tightened just long enough to cause pain and then loosened again before inflation was beaten. People came to expect inflation, and expectations started to drive it.
Volcker breaks the fever

In August 1979 President Jimmy Carter appointed Paul Volcker to chair the Federal Reserve. On October 6, 1979, Volcker announced a new approach that let interest rates rise as high as needed to slow money growth. The federal funds rate, the Fed's key rate, reached close to 20% in 1980 and 1981. Mortgage rates went above 18%.

The cure was brutal. The US went through two recessions in quick succession. Unemployment reached 10.8% at the end of 1982. Farmers drove tractors to Washington to protest. But inflation fell to around 3% by 1983, and the Fed earned back its credibility. A 40-year era of falling interest rates began, which Chapter 9 calls the long bond summer.

rows: The dollar became a pure promise
Currencies traded freely, oil prices quadrupled

blocks.text: The owner's Ledger Age series listed five effects of 1971: the dollar became a pure promise, unlimited printing became possible, inflation became the default, the petrodollar arrived, and cheap credit flowed to those who could borrow and buy assets. All five are well supported, with one sharpening. Printing became possible without a gold limit, but it is not unlimited in practice. The limits moved from metal to politics and markets: how much inflation voters will tolerate, and how much debt the bond market will absorb at what price. Volcker proved the limit is real when it is enforced.

blocks.q: After 1971, what does the dollar's value rest on, if not gold?
blocks.a: On trust in the US government and its taxing power, the size and openness of the US economy, the Fed's management of interest rates and inflation, and the network effect of the whole world already using dollars.

blocks.q: Who gained and who lost in the 1970s inflation?
blocks.a: Borrowers with fixed-rate loans and owners of real assets like gold, land and oil gained. Savers in cash and bonds, people on fixed incomes and workers whose wages lagged prices lost.

rules: A temporary suspension of a money promise often becomes permanent. Plan for that.
When a currency has no metal anchor, its limit is political. Watch inflation tolerance and bond market patience.
Inflation that people come to expect is far harder to stop than inflation that surprises them.

connects.how: The Triffin dilemma from Chapter 3 is what finally broke in 1971.
Oil money slotted into the recycling loop from Chapter 4.
Credit expansion became structural once the gold brake was gone.
The 1970s are the clearest inflationary season of the last century.

chapters.title: How money is born today
chapters.kicker: Most new money is not printed by the government. It is typed into existence by a bank when it makes a loan.

blocks.text: With gold gone, where does new money come from? Most people imagine a government printing press. That picture is mostly wrong. This chapter shows the actual machinery, step by step, with a simple set of books. It is the chapter to reread if any later one feels confusing.
Three kinds of dollars
Not all dollars are the same kind of thing. There are layers, each a promise from a different promiser.

rows: Base money: paper cash and bank reserves
Cash: anyone. Reserves: only banks and a few institutions with Fed accounts
Anyone, through a broker or bank
About $31.8 trillion of marketable debt held by the public

blocks.text: The money you use day to day is almost all the second layer: bank deposits. When you pay with a card or an app, you are moving bank deposits. Paper cash is a small share.
Loans create deposits
In 2014 the Bank of England, the central bank of the United Kingdom, published a short paper that surprised many readers. It described what bankers already knew.
Whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit in the borrower's bank account, thereby creating new money.
blocks.by: Bank of England, Money creation in the modern economy, 2014

blocks.text: A bank does not lend out a pile of savings it was holding. It writes two new entries in its books at the same moment. Let us watch it happen.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.text: Maria borrows $20,000 from her bank to buy a car. Before the loan, the bank's books show nothing about Maria. The moment the loan is approved, the bank adds an asset: a $20,000 loan that Maria owes the bank. It also adds a liability: a $20,000 deposit in Maria's account that the bank owes Maria. Both sides grow by $20,000. Maria's own books mirror this: she now has a $20,000 deposit (an asset) and a $20,000 debt (a liability). No one else's deposit went down. The economy has $20,000 more money than it had a minute ago.

blocks.caption: Double-entry: the bank records a new loan as an asset and a new deposit as a liability at the same instant. The deposit is new money.

items: Maria pays the car dealer. Her deposit moves to the dealer's account, maybe at another bank.
Between the two banks, the payment settles in reserves at the Federal Reserve. Banks keep reserve accounts at the Fed for exactly this.
The dealer now has $20,000 in deposits. The money keeps circulating, paying wages, suppliers and taxes.
As Maria repays the loan, her payments cancel both her debt and an equal amount of deposits. Repaying a bank loan destroys money, just as making one created it.

blocks.text: When you deposit your paycheck, you are lending money to your bank. Your deposit is the bank's debt to you. You are an unsecured lender, protected by government deposit insurance up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category. This is why bank runs happen: depositors are creditors who can all ask for their money back at once.
What limits banks, then?
If banks can create money by lending, why not lend infinitely? Because lending has real limits, just not the ones in the old textbook.

items: Capital rules: regulators require banks to fund a share of their loans with their owners' money, so losses hit shareholders first.
Borrower demand: someone has to want the loan and be judged able to repay it.
Profit: the loan must earn more than it costs the bank to fund and manage.
Interest rates: the Fed sets the price of reserves, which ripples out to the price of every loan. Higher rates mean fewer borrowers.

blocks.myth: Banks can lend about ten times their reserves, so every dollar of base money becomes ten dollars of loans.
blocks.reality: This is the old money multiplier from textbooks, and the owner's notes used it, for example multiplying gold or Bitcoin by ten. The Bank of England's 2014 paper, which the owner also cites, says the reverse: banks lend first, and the central bank supplies reserves as needed at its chosen interest rate. In the United States, reserve requirements have been zero since March 2020. There is no fixed multiplier. The binding limits are capital, demand, profit and the interest rate. The owner's instinct that money is debt is correct. The fixed ten times rule is not.

blocks.text: The government's part: the Treasury

The US Treasury is the government's money manager. It keeps its main checking account, the Treasury General Account, at the Federal Reserve. In mid-October 2026 it held about $886 billion. When the government spends, say on a Social Security payment, money moves from that account to the recipient's bank. The recipient's deposit rises and the bank's reserves at the Fed rise. Government spending adds money to the private economy.
When you pay taxes, the reverse happens. Your deposit falls, your bank's reserves fall, and the Treasury's account at the Fed rises. Taxes drain money out of the private economy.

Because the government spends more than it taxes, it borrows the difference. It does this through primary auctions. Treasury announces how many bills, notes and bonds it will sell. A group of about two dozen large banks, called primary dealers, must bid. Pension funds, money market funds, foreign central banks and individuals bid too, directly or through the dealers. Buyers pay with deposits and reserves, which move into the Treasury's account.

The Fed is not allowed to buy new Treasuries straight from the government at auction, apart from rolling over bonds it already owns. When the Fed does buy Treasuries, it buys them from banks and investors in the open market. That is what quantitative easing was: the Fed creating reserves to buy bonds that were already out there.
The owner's loop, corrected and kept

The owner sketched the money circuit as Treasury to Fed to banks to public to IRS (the tax office) to Treasury. That is a real loop, and the core insight, that modern money is a circuit of debts, is right. Here it is with the parts in their correct places.

items: Congress decides spending and taxes. Treasury spends from its account at the Fed, which adds deposits for the public and reserves for their banks.
Treasury covers the gap between spending and taxes by auctioning Treasury securities to dealers, banks, funds, foreigners and individuals, not to the Fed directly.

Banks create most new money by making loans to households and businesses. The Fed does not hand banks money to lend. It sets the interest rate on reserves and lends to banks against good collateral when needed.
The public spends, saves and repays loans. Repaying bank loans destroys deposits.
The public pays taxes to the IRS, which moves deposits and reserves back into Treasury's account at the Fed.
The Fed sometimes buys or lets run off Treasury securities in the open market, and when it makes a profit it sends it to the Treasury.

blocks.text: The owner also wrote that the Fed controls the speed of credit expansion, not the amount. That is close to right. The Fed sets the price of money, the interest rate, and banks and borrowers decide the quantity at that price. In September 2026 the Fed, now chaired by Kevin Warsh, raised its target rate to 3.75 to 4.00%, a sign that it is trying to slow the speed.

blocks.q: Maria repays her entire $20,000 car loan. What happens to the money supply?
blocks.a: It shrinks by $20,000. Her repayment cancels both her loan, an asset of the bank, and an equal amount of deposits, a liability of the bank. Money created by a loan is destroyed when the loan is repaid.

blocks.q: Does the Federal Reserve lend money to the Treasury when the government runs a deficit?
blocks.a: Not directly. The Treasury borrows by selling securities at auction to dealers and investors. The Fed may later buy some of those securities in the open market, which is one reason people say the Fed finances deficits indirectly.

rules: Most money is bank credit. Every deposit is somebody's loan somewhere.
A loan creates money, and repaying it destroys money. Watch both directions.
Do not trust a fixed money multiplier. Watch capital, demand and the interest rate instead.

connects.how: This is the modern form of the ledger from Chapter 1: money as a record of debts.
Because repaying loans destroys money, the musical chairs worry comes next.
Stablecoins add a new layer on top of these three, backed by the Treasury layer.

chapters.title: Bonds: the backbone of today's money
chapters.kicker: If you do not understand the government bond, you do not understand modern money, because modern money is built on top of it.

blocks.text: Chapter 6 showed that banks create money when they lend. This chapter is about the thing almost all of that money ultimately leans on: the government bond. Most people skip bonds because they sound boring. That is exactly why so few people understand where interest rates, mortgages, stablecoins and even currency power come from.
What a bond is, in one breath

A bond is an IOU with a schedule. The government borrows $1,000 today and promises to pay you a fixed amount every year (the coupon) and your $1,000 back on a set date (maturity). US Treasury bills last a year or less and pay no coupon: you buy them below face value and get the full amount back. Notes last 2 to 10 years and bonds 20 to 30 years. The US has about $32.57T of this debt held by the public, and about 22% of the tradable part is short-term bills.
Why bonds sit underneath everything

items: The Fed's money rests on them. The Fed creates bank reserves and cash, and the main asset it holds against them is Treasuries (about $4.57T).
They are the financial system's pawnshop ticket. In repo markets, banks and funds hand over Treasuries overnight to borrow cash. Trillions move this way every day.
Banks and money funds park cash in them, because rules treat them as the safest liquid asset.
Stablecoins must hold them. Under the GENIUS Act, every compliant dollar token has to be backed by bills of 93 days or less.
Foreign central banks keep their savings in them. That is how the world holds dollars without holding cash.
They set the base price of money. Mortgages, car loans and company loans are priced as the Treasury yield plus a margin for risk.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of money as a tower of glasses at a wedding, the kind where champagne is poured into the top glass and overflows downward. Government bonds are the bottom row. Every glass above, from bank deposits to stablecoins to your mortgage, rests on that row. If the bottom row wobbles, the whole tower shakes.
The seesaw: why price and yield move in opposite directions

blocks.caption: A bond's coupon is fixed. When new bonds pay more, old bonds must get cheaper to compete, so price falls as yield rises.

items: You buy a $1,000 bond that pays $50 a year. Your yield is 5%.
Next month the government sells new bonds paying $60 a year on $1,000, a 6% yield.
Nobody will pay $1,000 for your $50 bond when a $60 one is on offer. To sell it, you must cut the price until $50 a year is also about 6% of what the buyer pays: about $833.
Your bond lost about $167 of market value, even though the government never missed a payment. That is price risk, and it is why 'safe' bonds can still lose money.

blocks.text: What moves the yield: the price of patience
A bond yield is the price of patience. It is what the market demands for handing over money today and waiting for it to come back. Seven forces set that price.

rows: Short yields track where the Fed sets overnight rates now and where markets expect it to go
Expected hikes push yields up, expected cuts pull them down
Lenders want compensation for prices rising while they wait
More expected inflation means higher yields
Extra pay for locking money up for years when the future is uncertain
More uncertainty about deficits, inflation or policy pushes long yields up
How much the Treasury must borrow and in what lengths
Bigger deficits and more long bonds push yields up
Who must or wants to buy: foreign central banks, banks, money funds, pensions, stablecoins
Captive or eager buyers pull yields down, a big seller pushes them up
A strong economy competes for money, a weak one frees it up
Booms raise yields, recessions lower them
Confidence in repayment and in the value of the currency repaid
Any doubt raises yields, a crisis elsewhere can lower them as money flees to safety

blocks.caption: The US 10-year yield of 5.13% on 2026-10-21 split into its two big parts, using market prices.

blocks.text: You can see several forces at once in 2026. The Fed hiked in September (force 1). Oil above $100 kept inflation worries alive (force 2). A $1.99T deficit meant heavy issuance (force 4). Japan sold $171B of Treasuries to defend the yen (force 5). Meanwhile French stress pushed some European money into Treasuries for safety (force 7 in reverse). The result: a 10-year yield of 5.13% and a 30-year mortgage at 7.40%.
The yield curve: a weather vane

Line up yields from short to long and you get the yield curve. Normally it slopes up, because waiting longer deserves more pay. In October 2026 it does: about 4.81% at 2 years, 5.13% at 10 years and 5.42% at 30 years. When short yields rise above long ones (an inverted curve), markets are betting the Fed will have to cut, usually because a slowdown is coming. Inversions have preceded most US recessions, though the timing is loose.

blocks.myth: Government bonds are safe, so you cannot lose money on them.
blocks.reality: They are safe from default, not from price changes. In 2022 bonds had one of their worst years on record. In March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failed largely because the long Treasuries and mortgage bonds it held had fallen in price as rates rose. Safe means the promise will be kept, not that the price will hold.

blocks.text: I used to think if there was reincarnation, I wanted to come back as the president or the pope or as a .400 baseball hitter. But now I would want to come back as the bond market. You can intimidate everybody.
blocks.by: James Carville, adviser to President Clinton, 1993

blocks.text: The bond market is the only voter that votes every second. When it dislikes a government's plans, yields rise and the government's own interest bill rises with them. US net interest reached $1,051.8B in FY2026, more than defense. That bill is the bond market's running verdict, and it is why Treasury secretaries watch auctions more closely than polls.

blocks.q: If the Treasury suddenly has to sell far more long bonds while its biggest foreign buyer is selling, what happens to long yields and to mortgage rates?
blocks.a: Supply rises and demand falls, so bond prices drop and yields rise. Mortgages are priced off long Treasury yields, so mortgage rates rise too.

rules: Government bonds are the bottom row of the money tower. Learn them and the rest of the tower makes sense.
Price and yield move in opposite directions. Safe from default is not safe from loss.
A yield is the price of patience, set by the Fed path, inflation, uncertainty, supply, demand, growth and trust.

connects.how: Banks create deposits, and bonds are the assets that most of that money ultimately leans on.
Foreign surpluses come back to the US as Treasury purchases.
Stablecoins and tokens are new glasses on the same bottom row of bonds.

chapters.title: The musical chairs question
chapters.kicker: If all money is borrowed and interest is owed on top, can everyone ever pay? The honest answer is yes in a quiet world, and not always in a real one.

blocks.text: Chapter 6 showed that money is born as debt. That raises a question almost everyone hits sooner or later, and the owner of this project put it in a sharp form.
Imagine I give a person my own currency YYY$10, but I tell them they must pay me back 5% interest, but no matter how much they work they can't repay if there is only YYY$10 in circulation.
blocks.by: The owner of this project, in their own words

blocks.text: It feels like musical chairs. Ten chairs, ten and a half people. Someone must always be left standing, or someone must always borrow more to keep the music playing. Let us test the intuition carefully, because it is half right, and the half that is right matters a great deal.

blocks.caption: The worry: YYY$10 in circulation, YYY$10.50 owed. If the stock of money is all there is, someone must default or borrow more.

blocks.text: Why it feels impossible
The worry treats money as a fixed pile, a stock. You hand out 10. You ask for 10.50 back. There are only 10 in existence. Arithmetic seems to say no.

The missing piece is time. Money is not used once. It moves. The same coin can pay many debts in a year, because each person who receives it spends it again. Economists call how often money changes hands its velocity. Debts are paid from flows over time, not from the stock all at once.
The real mechanism: the lender spends

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: You are the lender on a small island. You lend YYY$10 to Bea, a fisher, at 5% a year. Each year Bea owes you YYY$0.50 of interest. Where does she get it? From you. You need to eat, so you buy YYY$0.50 of fish from Bea each year. She takes that YYY$0.50 and pays you the interest. Next year, the same thing. The money supply never changes. It stays at YYY$10. Bea pays her interest forever. Nobody is left standing.

Interest is a payment for a service, the use of money over time. As long as the person who receives interest spends it back into the economy, on goods, wages, rent or taxes, the money circulates and can be earned again. Even repaying the principal is possible. Bea can sell you more fish over time and pay down the YYY$10. When she finishes, the money she borrowed is gone, because the loan that created it is gone. That is not a failure. It is the loop from Chapter 6 running in reverse.

Economists who modeled this carefully, including critics of mainstream economics such as Steve Keen, have shown that a pure credit economy can pay interest in a steady state without needing endless new loans. So the strict version of the musical chairs claim, that interest can never be paid without more debt, is not correct.

blocks.myth: Because banks only create the principal and never the interest, the system needs ever more debt just to pay interest, or it collapses.
blocks.reality: Interest is paid out of the circulating flow of money, and banks spend their interest income on salaries, rent, dividends and taxes, which puts it back into circulation. In a steady state, interest can be paid indefinitely. The real dangers come from somewhere else, and they are listed below.

blocks.text: Where the intuition is right
Now the important part. The owner's instinct points at real weaknesses. They are just different from the arithmetic one.

items: Savers who do not spend. If the people receiving interest save it instead of spending it, money piles up with them and drains from everyone else. If savers as a group want their savings to keep growing, someone else must keep going deeper into debt. This is an accounting fact, made famous by the economist Wynne Godley: for every saver accumulating financial assets, some sector, households, businesses, government or foreigners, must be adding debt.

Debt can outgrow income. Paying interest is possible. Paying more and more interest on debts that grow faster than incomes is not sustainable. Global debt is about $365 trillion, roughly 310% of world output, according to the Institute of International Finance in 2026.
Repayment destroys money. If many borrowers try to pay down debt at once, deposits vanish, spending falls, prices and incomes drop, and the remaining debts get harder to pay.
Panics need cash now, not over time. In a crisis everyone wants to settle at once. Then the stock of money really is too small for the pile of claims, unless a central bank steps in.

blocks.text: The more the debtors pay, the more they owe.
blocks.by: Irving Fisher, The Debt-Deflation Theory of Great Depressions, 1933

blocks.text: Fisher saw this in the Great Depression. When everyone sells assets and cuts spending to repay debt, prices fall. Falling prices make each remaining dollar of debt heavier. Paying down debt can make debt burdens worse.
Minsky: stability breeds instability

The economist Hyman Minsky described three kinds of borrowers. Hedge borrowers can pay both interest and principal from income. Speculative borrowers can pay interest from income but must keep rolling over the principal. Ponzi borrowers cannot even pay the interest from income, and must borrow more or sell assets that they hope keep rising.

Minsky's key idea is that long calm periods push people from the first kind toward the third. Good times make lenders and borrowers confident, so they take on more debt against rising asset prices. Then a small shock, like a dip in house prices, reveals that many borrowers were Ponzi borrowers all along. The 2008 crisis is often called a Minsky moment, a phrase coined by economist Paul McCulley.

blocks.caption: The debt treadmill: when debt grows faster than income, the interest bill rises, so more borrowing is needed just to keep pace. Calm years tempt more people onto the faster belt.

blocks.text: Why credit growth became structural after 1971

Under gold, a bank boom eventually ran into a gold shortage and stopped. After 1971 that brake was gone. Each time a slump threatened, central banks could cut rates and governments could borrow, so recessions were shorter but debt rarely got cleared out. Over decades, debt grew faster than incomes. The system became like a bicycle that is stable only while it keeps moving forward.

The US government is the clearest current case. According to Treasury data gathered by this project, the government spent about $7.40 trillion in fiscal year 2026 and collected about $5.40 trillion, a deficit of about $1.99 trillion. Even before interest, it ran a primary deficit of about $941 billion, close to 2.9% of the economy. Interest itself cost about $1.05 trillion. The average rate on its marketable debt is about 3.5%, but new borrowing costs closer to 4.9%, and about 36% of the debt reprices within a year. Unless deficits shrink or rates fall, the interest bill climbs on its own.

The owner's notes say there is only about $15,000 of liquid money per person on earth against about $346 trillion of global debt, and conclude that we live in a world of scarce settlement capacity, not scarce money. The figures need updating: world broad money is now about $19,500 per person, and global debt is about $365 trillion. But the insight is sharp. Normally debts are paid slowly from flows, so a small stock of money services a huge stock of debt. In a panic, everyone wants settlement at once, and the stock is far too small. That is exactly why central banks act as lenders of last resort in a crisis.

blocks.q: In the island story, what single behavior would turn the YYY$10 economy into a real musical chairs game?
blocks.a: If you, the lender, stopped spending your interest and hoarded it. Then money would drain out of circulation into your savings, and Bea would eventually be unable to pay without borrowing more or defaulting.

blocks.q: Is it true that interest can never be paid without new loans?
blocks.a: No. In a steady state, interest can be paid indefinitely as long as interest income is spent back into circulation. The real risks are debt growing faster than income, savers hoarding, mass repayment shrinking the money supply, and panics.

rules: Interest can be paid from a circulating flow. Debt that grows faster than income cannot be paid forever.
When everyone repays at once, money shrinks and debts get heavier. Pace your debt so you never have to sell in a panic.
Calm years breed risky borrowing. Be most careful when lending feels safest.

chapters.title: The seasons of money
chapters.kicker: Money has weather. In some decades it melts, in others it hardens, and the same choice can make you rich in one season and poor in the next.

blocks.text: So far we have looked at how money is made. Now we look at how it behaves over time. Prices do not move in a straight line. They move in long seasons, some inflationary, some deflationary. Most people live through only two or three seasons, so they assume the one they grew up in is normal. The rulebook exists so you do not make that mistake.
Two kinds of weather

items: Inflation: prices in general rise, so each unit of money buys less. Debts get lighter in real terms. Savings in cash shrink in real terms.
Deflation: prices in general fall, so each unit of money buys more. Debts get heavier in real terms. Cash gains real value, but jobs and incomes usually suffer.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of money as ice. In a warm season, inflation, ice held in your hand melts, so you want to turn it into something that does not melt, like a house or a tool, and owing ice to someone is cheap because it shrinks while you owe it. In a cold season, deflation, ice keeps its shape and even grows, so holding ice is smart and owing ice is dangerous because your debt grows heavier.
A timeline of seasons, 1870 to 2026

blocks.caption: Seasons of money from 1870 to 2026: inflationary eras (wars, the 1970s, 2021 onward) and deflationary or disinflationary eras (1873 to 1896, 1929 to 1933, 1982 to 2020).

blocks.text: The last row comes from this project's 2026 data. US consumer energy prices rose about 20.4% over a year, oil traded near $98 a barrel in October, and a key inflation measure ran at 5.0% annualized in the second quarter. Real hourly pay fell about 0.7% in the year to September 2026. The Fed under Kevin Warsh raised rates in September 2026, against the President's wishes.

Financial repression is the polite name for a quiet trick governments use to shrink debt. They keep interest rates below inflation, so lenders to the government lose real value every year. Economists Carmen Reinhart and Belen Sbrancia showed in 2011 that the US and UK used this after the Second World War to cut their debt burdens substantially. A mild version is happening now: the average interest rate on US government debt is about 3.2 to 3.5%, while nominal income has grown about 5.7% a year over the past decade, so inflation is quietly shrinking the debt relative to the economy.
Why governments prefer mild inflation

items: It shrinks debt. A government that owes trillions benefits when each future dollar is worth a little less.
Wages are sticky downward. People resist pay cuts. With mild inflation, a business can let real wages adjust by giving smaller raises instead of cutting pay, which keeps more people employed.
It leaves room to cut rates. If inflation is 2% and rates are 4%, a central bank can cut rates enough to make borrowing cheap in real terms during a slump. With zero inflation, there is less room.
Deflation is scarier. Once people expect falling prices, they delay buying, firms delay hiring, and debts grow heavier. That spiral is hard to stop.

blocks.text: New Zealand adopted the first formal inflation target in 1990. The Federal Reserve formally adopted a 2% target in 2012. The owner calls inflation a circulation incentive, a leaking bucket that pushes people to spend or invest rather than hoard cash. That is a fair description of how a mild target works, and it is also why holding idle cash is a slow loss in most modern seasons.
Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

Friedman's line is famous and partly true. Over long periods, sustained high inflation does come with fast money growth. But most economists today add that supply shocks, like the oil embargoes of the 1970s or the 2026 energy shock, can drive prices up for a while even without fast money growth, and that expectations matter a great deal. Where scholars disagree is how much weight to give each.
Deflation traps

The United States from 1929 to 1933 is the classic trap. About 9,000 banks failed. The money supply fell by about a third, as Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz documented. Prices fell by about a quarter. Unemployment reached about 25%. Fisher's debt deflation, from Chapter 8, ran at full speed.

Japan is the modern case. After its stock and property bubble burst around 1990, banks were slow to admit losses, households and firms paid down debt for years, and prices drifted slightly downward for much of the period from the late 1990s to the early 2010s. The Nikkei stock index did not regain its 1989 peak until 2024. The economist Richard Koo called this a balance sheet recession: everyone repaying debt at once, so nobody borrows to spend.
A store of value changes jobs with the season
Here is a subtle point that most people never notice. An asset is not simply safe or risky. It is a tool that works in some seasons and fails in others.

blocks.text: Gold is usually called an inflation hedge, but from 1980 to 2001, a period that still had inflation, gold lost most of its value in real terms. What gold really hedges is a loss of trust in the money or the people managing it. When trust is high and real interest rates are high, gold tends to struggle. When trust falls, gold shines. In 2025 central banks bought about 863 tonnes of gold, a sign that some governments trust the system less.

blocks.myth: There is one safe asset you can buy and forget.
blocks.reality: Safety depends on the season. Long-term US government bonds are free of default risk, but holders lost close to half their market value from 2020 to 2023 as rates rose. Cash is safe from crashes but loses value to inflation. The most reliable protection is to understand which season you are in and to avoid betting everything on one season continuing.

blocks.q: You have a fixed-rate mortgage and inflation jumps to 8%. Are you better or worse off in real terms?
blocks.a: Better off as a borrower, as long as your income keeps up. Your fixed payments and remaining debt shrink in real terms because each dollar you repay buys less.

blocks.q: Why did Japan's long stagnation happen even though interest rates were near zero?
blocks.a: Households, firms and banks were focused on repairing their balance sheets after the 1990 bust, so they paid down debt instead of borrowing to spend. Cheap money did not help when nobody wanted to borrow.

rules: Know your season. Ask whether money is melting or hardening before you decide to save, borrow or invest.
Mild inflation is the default policy goal. Idle cash slowly loses in most modern seasons.
No asset is safe in every season. Spread your bets across seasons, not just across names.
