chapters.title: The deflation debate: would anyone spend a money that grows?
chapters.kicker: If a dollar buys more tomorrow, why spend it today? The oldest argument against hard money, why it never ends, and what both sides miss.

blocks.text: Chapter 9 showed that money has seasons. This chapter takes one question from the cold season and follows it all the way down, because it sits under almost every fight about gold, Bitcoin and central banks. The question is simple: if I know my $1 will buy more tomorrow, why would I spend it today?
The case against a growing money

items: Prices are expected to fall, so people wait to buy cars, homes and machines.
Shops and factories sell less, so they cut prices further and cut jobs.
Workers who lose income spend even less. Borrowers find their debts heavier, because the money they owe is worth more while their income shrinks.
Defaults rise, banks pull back, and the loop feeds itself. Economists call this a deflationary spiral. Irving Fisher described its debt side in 1933 and called it debt deflation.

blocks.text: This is why almost every major central bank aims for a little inflation, usually 2%, rather than zero or falling prices. The cases they point to are the Great Depression and Japan's lost decades, both in chapter 9.
The case for a growing money

items: You still need things today. Food, rent, medicine and school fees do not wait. People keep buying phones and televisions even though they know next year's model will be cheaper and better.
Waiting has a cost. A sofa you buy next year is a year without a sofa. Economists call this time preference: people value having things sooner.
History has good deflations. From the 1870s to the 1890s US prices fell for years while output, railways and industry grew fast, because new technology made things cheaper to produce.

The data are weaker than the fear. A 2015 Bank for International Settlements study covering about 140 years and up to 38 economies found only a weak link between falling consumer prices and slower growth, mostly driven by the Great Depression. The damage came mainly from falling property prices combined with private debt.
Discipline. When money cannot be printed, governments and companies must fund projects from real savings, so fewer bad projects get started.

blocks.text: Why the fight never ends: two sides, two different deflations

blocks.caption: The same falling prices with opposite causes. Good deflation starts with cheaper production. Bad deflation starts with collapsing demand and heavy debt.

blocks.text: The argument goes in circles because each side pictures a different deflation. The hard-money side pictures good deflation: things get cheaper because we got better at making them, incomes hold steady, and every paycheck buys more. The central-bank side pictures bad deflation: prices fall because nobody is buying, while debts stay fixed. Both have happened. Which one you get depends mostly on one thing: how much debt is in the system when prices start to fall.

Today's world carries record debt. The US government alone owes $40.44T. In a deflation every one of those dollars gets heavier to repay. That is the real reason no heavily indebted government will choose a deflationary money. The debate sounds like it is about shoppers delaying purchases. Underneath, it is about who carries the debt.
Spend the worse money, keep the better one

An older rule explains what people actually do when they can choose between two monies. It is Gresham's law: bad money drives out good. People spend the money that is losing value and hoard the one that is gaining. In Tudor England people spent the clipped and debased coins and kept the full-weight ones at home.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: On 22 May 2010 a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, the first well-known purchase of real goods with Bitcoin. At about $86,000 a coin in early October 2026, those coins would be worth roughly $860 million. After stories like that, almost nobody spends Bitcoin on pizza. They spend dollars and keep the Bitcoin. That is Gresham's law in a single slice.

So a money expected to grow tends to become a store of value, while a money that slowly melts becomes the one people spend. That is why the medium of exchange argument against deflationary money is partly right and partly beside the point. People do not stop spending. They spend the other money. Today that other money is the dollar, or a dollar stablecoin, sitting next to gold or Bitcoin in the same wallet.

blocks.myth: Falling prices always mean a weak economy.
blocks.reality: Prices of televisions, computers and phones have fallen for decades while the industries making them boomed. What hurts is falling prices plus heavy debt plus collapsing demand, not falling prices alone.

blocks.text: This matters for the future this desk studies. Robots, AI and cheap solar push the cost of making things down, a good-deflation force. A debt-heavy system cannot let that show up as falling prices, so it creates enough new money to keep prices rising gently. The productivity gain does not vanish. It flows to whoever receives the new money first and to owners of scarce things such as land, energy and platforms. That is the link to the Cantillon effect and the platform toll booths in chapter 17.

blocks.q: If prices are expected to fall 2% a year, why might a family still buy a fridge today?
blocks.a: Because it needs a fridge now. Waiting a year to save 2% means a year without a fridge. Real needs and time preference keep spending going. A spiral starts when incomes fall and debts bite, not from cheaper prices alone.

blocks.q: Why do most people spend dollars and keep gold or Bitcoin?
blocks.a: Gresham's law. When two monies circulate side by side, people spend the one expected to lose value and hoard the one expected to gain.

rules: A deflation is good or bad depending on its cause and on how much debt sits in the system.
People do not stop spending when one money grows. They spend the other money and keep the growing one.
The fight over inflation is a fight over who carries the debt.

chapters.title: Why empires and their currencies fall
chapters.kicker: No money has ruled forever. The ones that fell usually fell the same way: war, debt and a slow watering down of the promise.

blocks.text: The dollar has been the world's main money for about a century. Before it, other currencies held that role and lost it. This chapter walks through the most famous cases, looks for the common pattern, and then asks honestly what is different today. It is the chapter where humility matters most, because history rhymes but never repeats exactly.
Rome: the long watering down

Chapter 2 told the story of the denarius. Rome's army and borders were enormously expensive. As conquest slowed, new silver stopped arriving, but the bills kept coming. Emperors filled the gap by debasing the coin. By the late 200s AD the coinage had collapsed, prices had soared and the state increasingly collected taxes in goods rather than in its own worthless coins.

The story has a twist that few people know. The emperor Constantine introduced a gold coin, the solidus, in the early 300s. In the eastern half of the empire, which became Byzantium, the solidus kept its gold content for roughly 700 years, until it was debased in the 1000s. It was the dollar of the medieval Mediterranean. A money can stay honest for centuries when the state that issues it chooses to keep it so.
Spain: rich in silver, poor in the end

In 1545 Spanish colonizers found a mountain of silver at Potosi, in today's Bolivia. Silver from Potosi and Mexico flooded into Spain for over a century, and the Spanish silver coin, the piece of eight, became a world money used from China to the American colonies.

Yet the Spanish crown went bankrupt again and again. Philip II stopped payments to his bankers in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596. The silver was spent on wars across Europe and on imports, and it flowed out as fast as it came in. Prices across Europe rose several-fold over the 1500s, an episode called the price revolution. Historians still debate how much of that inflation came from American silver and how much from population growth. What is clear is that easy money without a productive base did not make Spain lastingly strong.
The Dutch: the first modern financial center

In the 1600s the small Dutch Republic became the trading and financial center of Europe. Amsterdam created the Dutch East India Company in 1602, one of the first companies with tradable shares, and the Bank of Amsterdam in 1609, whose bank money was trusted across Europe. Dutch guilders and bills of exchange financed world trade.

Decline came through a mix of costly wars with England and France, rising debt, and loss of trading edge as Britain grew. A disastrous war with Britain from 1780 to 1784 hit hard. It later emerged that the Bank of Amsterdam had secretly lent heavily to the struggling East India Company and the city, which undermined trust in its money. The company was dissolved in 1799 and the bank was wound down in 1819.
Britain: the pound sterling

Britain built the most successful money of the 1800s. The Bank of England, founded in 1694, and the gold standard of Chapter 2 made sterling the currency of world trade and London the world's banker. Britain carried enormous debt after the Napoleonic Wars, more than twice its economy, but the Industrial Revolution grew the economy fast enough to carry it. High debt alone did not sink Britain.

Two world wars did. Britain sold overseas investments and borrowed heavily from the United States to fight. After 1945 it was a large debtor with a weakened industry. The decline of sterling then took decades: a convertibility crisis in 1947, American financial pressure during the Suez crisis of 1956, a devaluation in 1967, and a loan from the IMF in 1976. The economist Barry Eichengreen showed that the dollar actually overtook sterling as a reserve currency as early as the mid-1920s, fell back in the 1930s, and only pulled clearly ahead after the Second World War. Changes at the top are slow and messy, not sudden.
The common pattern

blocks.caption: A common pattern in past declines: rising power and trust, a peak with a trusted currency and financial center, then war costs, rising debt, debasement or inflation, and a rival taking the lead. A framework, not a law.

items: A rising power wins trust through productive strength, trade and sound money.
Its currency becomes the world's preferred money, and its capital becomes the financial center. Borrowing becomes cheap.
Cheap borrowing funds wars, overseas commitments and consumption. Debt rises faster than the productive base.
To pay the bills, the state debases its coin or inflates its paper, and trust starts to fade.
A rival with stronger production offers an alternative. The center of money moves, usually after a great war.

blocks.text: A popular chart, often shown by investment firms, lists the leading currencies of the last 600 years with lifespans of roughly 80 to 110 years each: Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, France, Britain and the United States. Treat it with care. Historians argue about whether reserve currency even means much before the 1800s, the dates are rough, and as the sterling story shows, top currencies often share the stage for decades. The chart is a conversation starter, not a countdown clock.
Dalio's big cycle: one framework

The investor Ray Dalio, in his 2021 book Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order, describes a big cycle of empires. He tracks measures such as education, innovation, competitiveness, economic output, share of world trade, military strength, financial center strength and reserve currency status. In his account, empires rise as education and innovation improve, peak when their currency and financial center dominate, and decline as debts mount, money is printed, wealth gaps widen, internal conflict grows and a rival rises.

The framework is useful because it makes you look at many measures at once. It is not a law of nature. Critics point out that the sample of empires is small, that the stages are easier to see in hindsight than in real time, and that very different histories get squeezed into one shape. Use it as a checklist for questions, not a calendar for predictions.
If something cannot go on forever, it will stop.
blocks.by: Herbert Stein, economist and adviser to Presidents Nixon and Ford, 1980s

blocks.text: What looks familiar now

items: Interest now costs more than defense. In fiscal year 2026 the US paid about $1,052 billion in net interest against about $965 billion for national defense, the third year in a row. The historian Niall Ferguson has argued that a great power spending more on debt service than on defense is a warning sign.
Debt rising faster than the economy. US debt held by the public is about 100% of GDP, and the deficit was about $1.99 trillion in 2026.
Allies hedging. Foreign official holdings of Treasuries at the New York Fed fell about $254 billion from February to October 2026, and central banks bought about 863 tonnes of gold in 2025.
A tax base leaning on wages. About 86% of federal receipts in 2026 came from individual income and payroll taxes, while machines and capital are taking a larger share of income.

blocks.text: What is genuinely different

items: No ready successor. The euro has no single government bond market and no single treasury behind it. China keeps controls on money leaving the country, which limits the yuan as a reserve. This project's research found that rivals' strongest cards today are in hardware, like rare earth magnets, batteries and solar technology, not in currency.

US debt is in its own currency. Spain owed its bankers in silver it could not create. The US owes dollars it can create. It is unlikely to default outright. The risk is inflation and higher interest rates, which is a slower, quieter kind of decline.
Digital rails may extend the dollar's reach. Most of the growth in dollar stablecoins went to holders outside the US, spreading dollar use rather than shrinking it.
Network effects are global and instant. Payments, oil, loans and contracts all run on dollar plumbing, and switching costs are enormous.

rows: S1: the dollar system extends, absorbing new rails
S2: a neutral layer (for example gold or a neutral token) gains a real role
S3: energy or compute becomes a monetary anchor

blocks.text: These are this project's own judgment, made in October 2026, not facts. Notice two things. The dollar stays the most likely single outcome for years. But the chance of something messier grows the further out you look. Both of those can be true at once.

blocks.q: What do Rome, Spain and Britain have in common in the decline of their money?
blocks.a: Each faced war costs and debts larger than their productive base could carry, leaned on debasement, borrowing or inflation to pay, and saw trust and leadership shift to a stronger rival.

blocks.q: Why is Dalio's big cycle a framework rather than a law?
blocks.a: It is based on a small number of historical cases, its stages are clearer in hindsight than in real time, and very different histories are fitted to one shape. It is useful for asking questions, not for predicting dates.

rules: Watch the ratio of interest to defense, and of debt to output. Those ratios have warned before.
Money centers move slowly and messily. Do not bet on a sudden collapse or on permanence.
A strong money needs a strong productive base. Easy money without production has never lasted.

connects.how: Rome's debasement and the gold standard's discipline are two ends of the same story.
The pillars of the dollar loop are what make this empire's currency different.
Debt outgrowing income, from the musical chairs chapter, is the engine of decline.
The rivals and new rails on today's board are the live test of this chapter.

chapters.title: The country leaderboard: deep markets and the game nations play
chapters.kicker: Why surplus nations park their savings in America, why climbing the leaderboard is so hard, and what it really took for each number one to get there and to fall.

blocks.text: Imagine every country on a leaderboard ranked by how much the world trusts its money. Near the top is a strange fact: some of the hardest working, highest saving nations on earth send a large share of their savings to the United States, a country that saves little and borrows a lot. To understand why, you need three ideas: deep markets, governance incentives and game theory.
What makes a market deep

A deep market is one where you can put in or take out enormous sums, quickly, at a fair price, and trust that the rules will not change on you. Few markets qualify. The US Treasury market is the deepest. Its qualities read like a checklist.

blocks.caption: The qualities that make savers worldwide choose one market over their own.

items: Size: tens of trillions of dollars of bonds, so even a central bank can buy or sell billions without moving the price much.
Liquidity: buyers and sellers are always there, every hour, through dealers, futures and repo.
Rule of law: independent courts, contracts that hold, and property that is not taken on a whim.
Open doors: money can leave whenever the owner wants. No exit queue, no permission slip.
A trusted central bank and a currency others already use for trade, debt and oil.
Hedging tools: futures, swaps and options let holders protect themselves.
Security: the military and alliances that protect trade routes and the system itself.

blocks.text: Notice the trade-off hidden in that list. The US gives up some control (it lets money in and out freely and lets courts bind the government) and in return earns the world's trust. Countries that want to keep tight control of their money cannot offer the same deal. That single trade-off explains much of the leaderboard.
Why surplus countries send their savings to America

When an exporter in Japan, China, Korea, Taiwan or the Gulf sells to the world, it earns dollars. If all those dollars were converted into local currency, the local currency would rise, exports would get dearer and factories would lose orders. So, often through the central bank, the dollars are kept as dollars and parked in the safest dollar asset available: Treasuries.

items: Stay competitive: holding the dollars instead of selling them keeps the home currency cheap and exports flowing.
Buy insurance: after the 1997 Asian crisis, countries that ran short of dollars were forced into painful IMF programs. Many vowed never again and built large dollar reserves.
No deep home alternative: many local bond markets are too small, too controlled or too easy to freeze to hold trillions.
Protect the wealthy: elites in less secure systems prefer assets where courts protect property, so private money follows the official money abroad.
Oil and commodities: these are priced in dollars, so exporters earn dollars and often recycle them through sovereign wealth funds.

blocks.text: How that trickles down into the home economy

Parking savings abroad is a governance choice, and ordinary citizens pay part of the bill. A deliberately cheap currency makes imports, fuel and foreign goods dearer for households. Savings that could have financed homes, wages or local businesses instead finance American borrowing. Exporters and the state gain, households consume less than they produce. On the other side, Americans enjoy cheap imports and cheap credit while factory towns hollow out, as chapter 4 showed. Each side's elite chose the arrangement, and each side's workers live with its costs.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Two neighbors. One works long hours, sells most of what it makes to the other, and lends the payment back so the other can keep buying. The lender's family lives modestly. The borrower's family lives well but its workshop goes quiet. Neither can easily stop: if the lender stops lending, its buyer disappears. If the borrower stops buying, the lender's factory stalls. That is the quiet bargain behind the dollar.

Economist Larry Summers called this mutual dependence a 'balance of financial terror' in 2004. Each side holds the other hostage, which is why sudden moves are rare and why the game is played with signals, slow shifts and patience.
The game theory of the leaderboard

blocks.caption: A currency war as a prisoner's dilemma. Each country is tempted to cheat, and if both do, both lose.

items: A coordination game: everyone uses the dollar because everyone else does. Switching only pays if many switch together, and the first to switch pays the most. That is why the leader keeps its place long after its advantages fade.

A prisoner's dilemma: each country gains by weakening its currency or adding tariffs, but if all do it, trade shrinks and all lose. The 1930s round of competitive devaluations and tariffs is the classic case.
A repeated game: nations meet again and again, so reputation matters. A country that keeps its promises can borrow cheaply for centuries. One that breaks them pays for decades.

A war of exhaustion: rivals drain each other through arms races, sanctions and tariff wars. History suggests leaders more often fall from overstretch and debt than from being overtaken in a single contest. Historian Paul Kennedy called this imperial overstretch.

The elite trap: a country rises on cheap labor and heavy investment, but climbing higher requires giving up control: floating the currency, opening the capital account, independent courts. The elites who profit from control often block those steps. Economists Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson describe this as extractive institutions resisting inclusive ones. It is one reason so many countries stall in the middle of the leaderboard.

blocks.myth: The country with the biggest economy automatically gets the top currency.
blocks.reality: Currency leadership lags economic leadership by decades. The US economy passed Britain's in the 1870s, yet sterling remained a leading reserve currency into the 1940s and beyond. Trust, habit and deep markets take generations to move.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern. Defaults and devaluations rarely end an empire in one blow. They are symptoms of a deeper strain: spending on war and status that the productive economy can no longer carry. France shows how fast it can turn political: a partial default in 1770 and a debt crisis in the 1780s led to the calling of the Estates General in 1789 and the Revolution.
What it really takes to be number one

items: Produce: a real economy that makes things the world wants.
Protect: security for trade routes and allies.
Promise: institutions that make debt credible, so the state can borrow cheaply in a crisis. Britain after 1688 and Hamilton's America after 1790 both won wars partly because lenders trusted them.
Plumbing: deep, open financial markets that others can use.
People: a culture of work, saving, invention and trust in contracts.
Place: geography that protects and connects, from Britain's channel to America's two oceans.

blocks.text: No single leader had all six forever. Each rose when its mix fit the technology and trade of its age, and each faded when debt, war and complacency ate the mix away. The open question for this century is whether the United States can keep its plumbing and promise strong enough to outlast the strain on the other pillars, and whether any rival is willing to give up enough control to offer a deeper market.

blocks.q: Why might a country with huge savings choose to lend them to the US instead of spending them at home?
blocks.a: To keep its own currency cheap for exporters, to hold insurance against a dollar shortage, because its home markets are too small or controlled to hold the savings, and because its elites trust US courts with their wealth. Its households pay part of the cost through dearer imports and lower consumption.

rules: Money flows to the deepest, safest, most open market, not the richest country.
A cheap currency helps exporters and taxes households. Ask who inside a country pays for its surplus.
Currency leadership lags economic leadership by decades, so do not expect sudden switches.
Empires rarely fall from one default. They fall when war and debt outgrow the productive base.

chapters.title: The view from a smaller currency: Malaysia, savings and where money lands first
chapters.kicker: Why a calm local price tag can hide a shrinking passport, how compulsory savings fund the home government, why talent and capital crowd into a few hubs, and whether Singapore was luck, strategy or someone else's plan.

blocks.text: Most of this Rulebook looks at money from the top, from Washington and the dollar. This chapter looks at it from the ground in a smaller economy. Malaysia is the worked example because its story touches every idea in this book, but the same logic applies to Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Turkey, South Africa and most of the roughly 180 currencies on earth.
The comfortable picture

A Malaysian worker sees a reassuring picture. Consumer inflation was 1.8% in September 2026 by the statistics department's count. The Employees Provident Fund (EPF), where most private-sector workers' retirement money must go by law, paid a 6.15% dividend for 2025 on investment assets of about RM1.41 trillion. Savings grow faster than prices. Why worry?
The picture is true, but it is measured with only one ruler: the ringgit, inside Malaysia. There is a second ruler most people never check.
Two rulers: the home price tag and the passport price tag

blocks.caption: What one ringgit buys abroad, then and now. Rates are approximate. The 1997 figures are before the Asian crisis.

blocks.text: Before the 1997 Asian crisis a US dollar cost about 2.50 ringgit. In October 2026 it costs about 4.08. So a ringgit buys roughly 39% fewer dollars than it did 29 years ago. Against the Singapore dollar the slide is steeper, from about 1.75 ringgit per Singapore dollar in early 1997 to about 3.2 in 2026. Inside Malaysia the loss is hidden, because local prices move gently. Outside, it shows up the moment you pay an overseas tuition bill, a foreign hospital, a holiday, an imported phone or anything priced in dollars.

items: Imported goods: fuel, food ingredients, machines, medicines and electronics are often priced in dollars. A weaker ringgit raises their cost in ringgit.
Education and health abroad: a family saving for a child's degree in the US or Britain is really saving in dollars or pounds, whatever its account says.
Travel and work options: the same salary buys fewer days abroad, and moving to a richer country costs more.
Assets priced globally: shares of global companies, gold and Bitcoin all cost more ringgit when the ringgit falls.

blocks.label: Be fair to both sides
blocks.text: Currencies swing both ways. The ringgit weakened to about 4.80 per dollar in early 2024, its weakest since the 1998 crisis, then strengthened to about 4.08 by October 2026. Short moves reverse. For a lifetime of savings the long trend is what counts, and since 1997 the passport ruler has shrunk.
Why the home price tag looks so calm

items: Subsidies and price controls. The government absorbs part of the cost of fuel, electricity and some foods. In September 2026, for example, protection on household electricity bills was widened from 600 to 800 kWh a month, which helped pull the utilities index down. The cost does not disappear. It moves onto the government's budget, and later onto taxes, debt or a subsidy cut.
The basket. Official inflation tracks an average household's local shopping. It does not include overseas school fees or the cost of moving abroad.
Local wages and rents set many prices, and they move slowly.

blocks.text: How Washington reaches a Malaysian wallet

items: The Fed raises rates or the Treasury sells more bonds, so dollar yields rise.
Global money leaves smaller markets to earn more in dollars, more safely. Foreign holders sell local bonds and shares.
The local currency falls. Imports get dearer, so inflation is imported even though nothing changed at home.
The local central bank must choose: raise its own rates to defend the currency, which hurts local borrowers and businesses, or let the currency fall and accept dearer imports.
Either way, households pay for a decision made in Washington. When the Fed eases or the dollar weakens, the flow reverses, which is part of why the ringgit strengthened in 2025 and 2026.

blocks.text: The rule no small economy can escape

blocks.caption: The impossible trinity. A country can hold only two corners at once. Each side of the triangle is a choice with a cost.

blocks.text: Economists call it the impossible trinity. A country cannot at the same time fix its exchange rate, let money flow freely in and out, and set its own interest rates. It must give one up. The US keeps free flows and its own rates, and lets the dollar float. Malaysia in September 1998 chose differently: it imposed capital controls and pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar, keeping control of its rates. The peg lasted until July 2005. Singapore chose a third path: it keeps money flowing freely and steers its exchange rate, and accepts that its interest rates largely follow world rates.
Captive savings: the EPF and the home government

The EPF is one of the largest pension funds in Asia, and also the biggest single holder of Malaysian government bonds, with about 28% of them according to the fund's statement for December 2023. Its policy is to place about 70% to 80% of new money inside Malaysia. About 39% of its assets were overseas in late 2025, and in 2024 the overseas part, about 37% of assets, earned about half of all investment income.

This is the same captive-demand playbook chapter 7 showed in Washington, where stablecoins are required by law to hold Treasury bills. A government with a large pool of compulsory savings has a reliable buyer for its debt at home. That keeps its borrowing cheap and its markets steady. The cost is that workers' retirement money is concentrated in the same economy that pays their wages, in the same currency.

To be fair, the EPF has done well in ringgit, and the leak is slower than many fear. The ringgit's fall against the dollar since 1997 works out to roughly 1.7% a year, so a 6% ringgit dividend is still very roughly 4% a year in dollar terms. The leak is real but quiet. It matters most for people whose future spending will happen abroad.
When the local economy hits bottom

The real test comes in a crisis. In 1997 and 1998 the ringgit fell from about 2.50 to about 4.88 per dollar at its worst in January 1998, roughly halving what Malaysian savings were worth in world terms within months. Stocks crashed, companies with dollar debts were crushed, and the government reached for capital controls. Malaysia recovered, but the lesson stayed: in a crisis, people with only local assets and a local passport have the fewest exits. People with income or savings in a strong currency, or skills that are paid in one, have options.

Malaysia remains deeply tied to the outside world. Its trade is larger than its whole economy, it is a key link in the world's chip supply chain, and its exporters earn dollars. That openness brought decades of growth. It also means a US recession, a tariff war or a Fed shock reaches Malaysian jobs within months. The same holds for most economies outside the few big hubs.
Why money and talent crowd into a few places

blocks.caption: New dollars ripple outward. The closer to the center, the earlier they arrive and the more they buy when they do.

blocks.text: Chapter 17 describes the Cantillon effect: whoever receives new money first spends it before prices rise. At world scale, new dollars are created in New York and Washington and land first in US banks, US markets and a handful of hubs such as London, Singapore, Hong Kong, Dubai and Zurich. Commodity exporters and factory economies receive them later, through trade. Households in smaller economies receive them last, often after their currency has already moved.

items: Capital goes where returns, rule of law and exits are best.
Talent follows capital, because that is where the jobs, the strong-currency salaries and the investors are.
Capital follows talent, because investors want to be near founders, engineers and deal makers.
The loop feeds itself. Each hub's lead makes the next arrival more likely. That is why successful businesses and entrepreneurs end up in the same few cities out of more than 190 countries.

blocks.text: Malaysia feels this loop directly. About 1.8 million Malaysians live abroad, and roughly 60% of them are in Singapore, according to a 2024 New Straits Times report citing World Bank work. The World Bank's chief economist Indermit Gill pointed to the currency gap as one reason educated Malaysians move there.
Singapore: anomaly, strategy, or someone else's plan?

Singapore is an island with no farmland, little water and no natural resources, separated from Malaysia in August 1965. Within two generations it became one of the richest places on earth. Some people decode this as a plan by American money managers to plant a financial outpost in Asia. Here is the record, run through this project's decoding method.

rows: 1961: Dutch economist Albert Winsemius leads a UN mission and becomes Singapore's long-time economic adviser
A home-grown plan with outside advice
1968: Singapore abolishes the tax on interest paid to foreign depositors. Bank of America opens the first Asian Currency Unit, starting the Asian Dollar Market
Singapore's government and a US bank, together
Singapore made itself the dollar's hub in the Asian time zone, and US banks were glad to use it
1971: the Monetary Authority of Singapore is set up. From 1981 monetary policy steers the exchange rate instead of interest rates
A deliberate choice inside the impossible trinity
1974 and 1981: Temasek and GIC are founded to invest national savings around the world
National savings sent abroad by design, unlike most countries
1990: an agreement gives US forces access to Singapore facilities. Changi Naval Base later hosts US aircraft carriers
A security umbrella traded for strategic usefulness
Location on the Strait of Malacca, one of the busiest sea lanes on earth
An advantage no plan could create

blocks.label: The decode verdict
blocks.text: Planted by American money managers: D3, folklore, about 10% likely as stated. No evidence shows Washington designed Singapore. Strategically welcomed by them: D1, decoded-strong, about 80% likely. Singapore's leaders deliberately made their island useful to the dollar system and to US security in Asia, and the US, its banks and its navy had every reason to support that. It was Singapore's plan, built to fit the American system. Small size let the plan be run tightly, and geography made it pay.

That is why Singapore is hard to copy. It needed a strategic location, leaders able to make long-term choices, rule of law trusted by foreign money, English as a working language, and the willingness to plug into the world's dominant system rather than fight it. Most countries have one or two of these. Very few have all of them at once.
Tying it together

items: A decision in Washington moves dollar yields.
Global money flows toward or away from smaller markets, and their currencies move.
Home inflation stays calm, partly because subsidies absorb the shock, while the passport price tag changes.
Compulsory savings such as the EPF recycle most local money into the home government and home market, in the home currency.
Money reaches the hubs first. Talent follows money, and money follows talent.
In a crisis, people with only local assets and local options have the fewest exits.
A few places, like Singapore, escaped by choosing to become hubs themselves. That took geography, discipline and decades.

blocks.myth: My country's inflation is only 2%, so my savings are safe.
blocks.reality: Safe on the home ruler. Measure them also on the passport ruler: what they buy in dollars, in a foreign degree or in the cost of moving. Both rulers matter, and the second one moves with decisions made abroad.

blocks.text: This is general education, not advice. The lesson people usually draw is to know which ruler their future spending will use. If your life will be lived at home, the home ruler matters most. If your children may study or work abroad, part of your savings is really owed in another currency. Skills that are paid in global terms are the most portable asset a person can own.

blocks.q: The Fed raises rates and the ringgit falls 10% against the dollar. Malaysian inflation stays at 2%. Has anything changed for a family saving for a child's degree in the United States?
blocks.a: Yes. The degree is priced in dollars, so it now costs about 11% more ringgit. The home price tag stayed calm, but the passport price tag rose.

rules: Measure your savings with two rulers: what they buy at home and what they buy abroad.
Money reaches the hubs first. Talent follows money, and money follows talent.
No country can fix its currency, open its doors to money and set its own rates all at once.

connects.how: Deep markets pull the world's savings toward the center.
Captive demand for government bonds, in Washington and in Kuala Lumpur.
The Cantillon effect at world scale.

chapters.title: The yardstick problem
chapters.kicker: We measure prices with money, but money itself keeps changing size. It is like measuring a room with a rubber ruler.

blocks.text: Chapter 9 talked about prices rising and falling. But compared to what? Every price is measured in money, and money's value is itself moving. This chapter gives you the tools to see through the moving ruler: nominal versus real, time prices, and the difference between consumer prices and asset prices.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Imagine measuring your child's height every year with a tape measure made of rubber that stretches a little each year. The marks say your child grew 10 centimeters. But the tape stretched 4. Your child really grew about 6. Money is that rubber tape. Every price, wage and savings balance you see is read off a tape that keeps stretching.

blocks.caption: A stretching yardstick: if the ruler (money) stretches, numbers rise even when the real thing has not grown. Real values strip out the stretch.

blocks.text: Nominal and real

items: Nominal means the number on the label, in today's money. Your salary is $50,000. A house costs $417,500.
Real means the number adjusted for the change in money's buying power, so you can compare across time.
The basic formula: real value equals nominal value divided by (1 plus inflation). The same idea works for growth rates: real growth is roughly nominal growth minus inflation.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.text: You earn $50,000. You get a 3% raise, to $51,500. Prices rose 5% over the same year. In last year's dollars your new pay is $51,500 divided by 1.05, which is about $49,048. Your nominal pay went up $1,500. Your real pay went down about $950, or about 1.9%. You can buy less than last year, even though your paycheck says you got a raise.

The same logic applies to savings. This project found that the average US savings account paid about 0.38% in 2026. With inflation running around 3.5% that year, the real return on that savings account was roughly minus 3% a year. A Treasury bill paying about 4.25% at the same time had a real return of a little under plus 1%. Both are very safe. The real results are very different.

When the news says the economy grew 5%, ask: nominal or real? In the second quarter of 2026 US nominal GDP grew at about an 8.5% annualized rate, but real GDP grew only about 2.2%. Most of the nominal growth was the ruler stretching.
Time prices: measuring in hours of life

One way around the rubber ruler is to measure prices in hours of work. How many hours must an ordinary worker labor to buy something? This sidesteps the changing size of the dollar, because wages and prices are both in the same money. The owner wrote, time is the real currency for now. Time prices take that seriously.

rows: Monthly payment on a median home

blocks.text: These figures come from this project's research, using the average hourly wage of production and nonsupervisory workers: about $10.20 in 1990 and $32.60 in September 2026. A few 1990 inputs are from memory sources and not perfectly verified, so read the house rows as approximate. The pattern, though, is strong and confirmed by independent studies.

Goods that can be made in factories and traded across borders keep getting cheaper in hours of work. Things tied to land, local services and institutions, like housing, health care and college, keep getting more expensive. Your hour buys more food and electronics than in 1990, and less of a house than in 2020. Most arguments about whether life is getting better or worse are really people looking at different halves of this table.
Asset inflation versus consumer inflation

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the prices of things people buy to use: food, rent, fuel, clothes, medical care. It does not include the prices of things people buy to own: stocks, bonds and houses as investments. For housing, CPI counts rent and an estimate of what owners would pay to rent their own homes, not the purchase price.

That gap matters. From February 2020 to 2026, average hourly pay rose about 32.5% and consumer prices about 30.3%, so real pay barely moved. Over a similar period, house prices rose about 59% and the S&P 500 stock index about 140%. If you only watch CPI, you miss that the price of entering ownership ran far ahead of pay.

blocks.myth: If inflation is low, your money is holding its value.
blocks.reality: Low consumer inflation means your money holds its value for buying groceries and gadgets. It says nothing about whether your money can still buy a house, a business or a share of the stock market. When new money flows mainly into assets, consumer inflation can stay modest while ownership slips out of reach. This is asset inflation, and it is invisible in the headline number.

blocks.text: Other rulers people propose

Some people say: measure everything in gold. Gold is not a stable ruler either. In the year to October 2026 gold went from a high of about $5,586 an ounce to about $4,131. Others say: measure everything in energy, such as kilowatt-hours. This project worked through the arithmetic. Because solar panels have become dramatically cheaper (module costs fell from about $132 per watt in 1975 to about $0.27 in 2024, in today's dollars), a fixed kilowatt-hour tends to buy less over time. Goods priced in kilowatt-hours would show inflation, not stability, while energy keeps getting cheaper.

There is no perfect ruler. The practical skill is to know which ruler you are using, and to check important decisions with more than one: dollars, real dollars, hours of work and perhaps a hard asset.

blocks.q: Your rent rises from $1,500 to $1,575 and your pay rises from $4,000 to $4,100 a month. Did rent take a bigger or smaller share of your pay?
blocks.a: Bigger. Rent went from 37.5% of pay to about 38.4%, because rent rose 5% while pay rose only 2.5%.

blocks.q: Why can house prices double while official inflation stays moderate?
blocks.a: Because the consumer price index counts rents and an estimate of owners' rental cost, not the purchase price of homes as assets. Asset prices can surge without showing up in the headline inflation number.

rules: Always ask: nominal or real? A raise below inflation is a pay cut.
Measure what matters to you in hours of work, not just dollars.
Watch asset prices as well as consumer prices. The price of ownership is the price of your future.

connects.how: The unit of account job from Chapter 1 is exactly this ruler.
Seasons only make sense once you correct for the moving ruler.
Asset prices outrunning pay is why the board game is hard to enter.
Energy as a ruler returns when we look at energy as collateral.

chapters.title: The new board game
chapters.kicker: In Monopoly the bank hands every player $1,500. In real life nobody does. So how does a new player get onto the board?

blocks.text: The owner asked a question that sits under every fear about the future of money.
If a new board game runs but no players have the starting money, how can a new player with no royal lineage and no inherited wealth start?
blocks.by: The owner of this project, in their own words

blocks.text: This chapter answers it in three parts: how money actually enters the board, the ladder of rungs a newcomer climbs, and what history says about times when the ladder was rebuilt. Then it looks at the routes open in 2026, using this project's own research.
How money enters the board
In Monopoly, every player starts with $1,500 from the bank. In the real economy there is no starting allowance. Chapter 6 showed the real doors through which money arrives.

items: Wages and sales: a business pays you for your work or buys what you make. This is the main door for most people.
Bank loans: a bank creates a deposit when it lends to you. This door opens only if a lender believes you can repay, often because you already have income or something to pledge.

Government spending and transfers: the government pays wages, contracts and benefits, which adds money to private hands. Programs like child tax credits, education grants and, in some proposals, universal income payments enter here.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: The real board game has no starting cash pile. Instead there are three ways onto the board. You can work for a player already on it, who pays you. You can persuade the bank to lend you chips, which usually requires showing chips you already have or wages coming in. Or the game's organizer can hand out chips, which happens rarely and in small amounts. Most players start through the first door, then use the chips they earn to climb.

blocks.caption: Entering the board: money arrives through wages and sales, bank loans, or government spending. Each door leads to the ladder: job, savings, credit, collateral, ownership.

blocks.text: The ladder of rungs

items: Job: trade time and skill for income. This gives you a flow of money.
Savings: keep part of that flow. This gives you a stock of money and a buffer against shocks.
Credit: a record of reliably repaying small debts. This lets lenders trust you with larger ones.
Collateral: an asset you can pledge, like a house deposit, equipment or a business's sales history. This unlocks cheaper and larger loans.
Ownership: a share of something that earns without your time, like a home, a business or stocks. This is where wealth compounds.

blocks.text: Each rung converts what you have into what you need for the next one. Wages become savings. Savings plus a repayment record become credit. Credit plus savings buy collateral. Collateral and its income become ownership. The owner's Ledger Age series describes three mindsets: the Worker chases today's cash, the Investor studies the maze, and the Architect borrows tomorrow's cash today, puts it to work and owns the maze. The ladder is the path from Worker to Architect.

blocks.myth: The Architect's play is simple: borrow at about 6% and invest in stocks that return about 13.6% a year.
blocks.reality: Borrowing to own assets is how many fortunes were built, and the owner is right that ownership, not wages, decides who keeps up. But the 13.6% is a recent ten-year average, not a promise. From 2000 to 2009 the S&P 500 returned roughly nothing. Borrowed money must be repaid on schedule even when assets fall, which is how the 2008 crisis ruined many leveraged owners. The Architect's rule of survival is to borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling.

blocks.text: When the ladder was rebuilt before

rows: Free land, the main productive asset of the age, for living on and farming it
About 270 million acres, about 10% of US land. Nearly 4 million claims, about 1.6 million completed deeds
Native nations whose land it was, and many Black Americans in practice
Public high school movement, about 1910 to 1940
A free credential that raised earning power
The share of young people with a high school diploma rose from about 9% to about half
Many Black students in segregated, underfunded schools

Many Black veterans, through local discrimination, and most women

blocks.text: Each reopening gave non-owners a productive asset or a credential that was large relative to the economy, and paired it with credit. Each also had exclusions, and the people left out became the next generation shut outside the board. The research of Raj Chetty and colleagues found that 90% of Americans born in 1940 out-earned their parents, against only about 50% of those born in the 1980s.
Today's routes, from this project's research

rows: Unemployment for ages 20 to 24 was 8.0% in September 2026, down from 9.2% a year earlier. Entry roles in fields exposed to AI are thinning, and recent graduates face 5.6% unemployment against 4.2% overall.
Under age 21, a credit card needs independent income or a cosigner. Realistic paths: authorized user on a parent's card, a secured card, or a credit-builder loan.

The broken rung. Median first-time home buyer age is a record 40. Saving a 10% down payment on a median home at 10% of young pay took about 6.2 years in 1990 and about 10 years now. About 49% of adults under 30 live with a parent.

The cheap but steep rung. A digital brand can launch for about $525 to $2,850, a small physical brand for about $1,900 to $7,400. But median solo founder revenue fell 23% in 2025 while the top tenth rose 19%, and platforms charge a growing toll for attention.

The bottom half of US households hold about 0.58% of directly held stocks and funds. Since late 2019, the top 10% took about 67.5% of the $78 trillion rise in household wealth, and the bottom half about 3.1%.

Trump Accounts give a $1,000 seed to children born 2025 to 2028. The seed alone grows to about $2,400 in today's money by 18 at 5% real return. Adding $50 a month reaches about $19,500. Today's 18-year-olds get no seed.

blocks.text: The owner worried that people living on a universal income would lose access to credit and assets, locking out their children. Under current law, this project found that worry is not supported: a steady benefit can count as income for a loan, roughly $69,000 of mortgage capacity per $1,000 a month. The real dividing line is not income source but ownership. Wage earners and benefit receivers are squeezed in the same places, housing, health cover and energy. The three tiers behave like two classes: owners, and people who depend on an income stream.
What actually moves a newcomer up

items: Get an income door open early, ideally in work that AI complements or that needs physical trust and licensing.
Build a thin credit file before you need it, and never miss a payment.
Own something from your first paycheck, even a small, diversified slice of the stock market. Ownership compounds while you sleep.
Treat a cheap business launch as a skills and equity lottery ticket, not a plan to quit everything.
Watch housing supply politics in your city. Broad, by-right zoning, as in Auckland after 2016, lowered rents in a measurable way. Land, not the house, is most of the price in expensive cities.

blocks.q: In the real economy, what are the three doors through which money reaches a new player?
blocks.a: Wages or sales from someone already on the board, loans from a bank that creates new deposits, and government spending or transfers.

blocks.q: What did the Homestead Act, public high schools and the GI Bill have in common?
blocks.a: Each gave non-owners a productive asset or credential that was large relative to the economy, often paired with credit, and each excluded some groups, who were left behind.

rules: There is no starting cash. Open an income door first, then climb: savings, credit, collateral, ownership.
Own something from your first paycheck. Ownership, not income, decides who keeps up.
Leverage is a ladder and a trapdoor. Borrow only what you can carry through a bad season.
Reopenings worked when they gave real assets at scale. Judge any new program by that test.

connects.how: The doors onto the board are the money creation channels of Chapter 6.
Asset prices outrunning pay is why the housing rung broke.
Tokens and new rails change how money moves, but not who owns the assets underneath.

chapters.title: Today's board: old anchors, new rails
chapters.kicker: The money in your app may look new, but under it sit the oldest anchors in the system: government bonds, bank credit and gold.

blocks.text: Every chapter so far has built toward this one. Here is the board as it stands in October 2026. The owner divided it into two sets. Set 1 is gold, Treasury bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is stablecoins, tokens and crypto rails. The big question is whether Set 2 replaces Set 1. This project's answer, after three rounds of research, is no. Set 1 is absorbing Set 2. In the project's phrase, it is an acquisition, not a merger.
The layers of money today

blocks.caption: The layers of money in 2026: gold at the base for nations, then central bank money, bank deposits and Treasuries, with tokens and stablecoins sitting on top and backed by Treasuries.

rows: Nothing but itself. No issuer, no promise
About 222,600 tonnes above ground, worth about $29.6 trillion. Central banks hold about 39,000 tonnes
Central banks as a neutral reserve, savers as insurance
The Fed's balance sheet and its legal authority
Fed total assets about $6.76 trillion. Bank reserves about $3.0 trillion
Banks, the government, and you through paper cash
The taxing power of the US government
Gross federal debt about $40.4 trillion. Marketable debt about $31.8 trillion
Everyone: foreign governments, banks, funds, stablecoin issuers
Bank loans, bank capital and deposit insurance up to $250,000
Households and businesses for daily money
By law, cash, bank deposits and Treasury bills of 93 days or less
About $304 billion, flat for a year. Tether about $183 billion, USDC about $73 billion
Traders, cross-border users, people in weak-currency countries
Scarcity by code and network belief, no issuer
About 20.1 million bitcoin at about $84,000, roughly $1.7 trillion
Holders seeking an asset outside the system

blocks.text: Set 1: three jobs, not one layer

items: Gold is the neutral reserve. It has no issuer to default and cannot be frozen if you hold it at home. Central banks bought about 863 tonnes in 2025. That buying rose after Russia's reserves were frozen in 2022.
Treasuries are the prime collateral. Stablecoins, banks, money funds and foreign governments all hold them. They are the asset that the rest of the system stands on.
Bank credit decides who can borrow against future income. A mortgage, a car loan or a first business loan still needs someone who studies your income and absorbs the loss if you fail.

blocks.text: Set 2: new rails on old anchors

Stablecoins are tokens on a blockchain that promise to be worth one dollar each. Under the US GENIUS Act, from January 18, 2027, every compliant stablecoin must be backed by cash, bank deposits or Treasury bills of 93 days or less. That means every new stablecoin dollar is new demand for Set 1 assets. Stablecoins cannot pay holders interest by law. And they cannot lend. They move money, they do not create credit.

Stablecoin issuers keep the interest. When you hold a dollar stablecoin, the issuer invests your dollar in Treasury bills and keeps the yield. Circle, the issuer of USDC, earned about $668 million of reserve income in one quarter of 2026 and paid about 61.5% of it to distribution partners such as Coinbase. Across the market, this float is worth roughly $11.7 billion a year at a 4.25% bill rate. Idle stablecoins cost you the interest you could have earned.

blocks.myth: Crypto will replace banks, so people with savings will stop borrowing from banks.
blocks.reality: Crypto is replacing some rails, how money moves and settles, not the balance sheet behind it. All crypto-backed lending was about $56 billion in mid-2026, roughly 0.4% of US bank loans, and it only lends against assets you already own. A loan against your future income still comes from a regulated lender. Banks are adapting too: JPMorgan launched a deposit token on a public blockchain in 2025.

blocks.myth: Bitcoin's 21 million coins, times ten, can support about $300 trillion of credit.
blocks.reality: That figure works out to bitcoin at the same total value as all gold, about $1.43 million per coin, then multiplied by ten. Real crypto lending runs the other way: borrowers pledge about $2 of crypto to borrow $1, and all crypto-backed lending is about 0.05 times bitcoin's value, not 10 times.

blocks.text: Digital central bank money

items: United States: a federal ban on a retail central bank digital currency is now law, carried in the same bill as a 2026 housing act. The Fed cannot issue a retail digital dollar. Digital dollars will come from private stablecoins and bank tokens.
Europe: a digital euro is under negotiation, with a holding cap of around 3,000 euros discussed and issuance in 2029 at the earliest.

China: the digital yuan, e-CNY, runs domestic pilots, including programmable payments that expire. The cross-border mBridge platform has settled about $55 billion in total. Saudi Arabia left it in May 2025.

blocks.text: Energy as collateral and ceiling

This project's central research question was whether energy will become money. The answer: energy will not replace the dollar you spend. It is taking over gold's old job as the scarce physical thing that caps how much real output any money can claim. In an economy of AI and robots, output grows with delivered electric power, and power cannot be printed.

Energy is also entering the system as collateral inside the dollar. Power plants, data centers, long electricity contracts and computer chips back new dollar loans. The project calls this the watt-dollar, a descendant of the 1974 petrodollar. US data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023, about 4.4% of US power, and projections for 2028 range from 325 to 580. Consumer energy prices rose about 20.4% in the year to September 2026.

blocks.caption: Energy as collateral and as ceiling: dollar loans are increasingly backed by power plants, data centers and chips, while delivered power caps how much real output money can buy.

blocks.text: Energy fails as everyday money because a kilowatt-hour is perishable, tied to a place, and keeps getting cheaper as solar spreads. Elon Musk's suggestion of a currency measured in watts and tonnage is closer to a post-scarcity accounting idea, similar to the 1930s Technocracy movement's energy certificates. Its real problem is the same as every planned money: who decides the allocations.

The rivals' strongest card is hardware, not currency. China's money moves, like selling some Treasuries or building alternative payment rails, have little bite so far. Its export controls on rare earth magnets, battery materials and, since October 2026, solar manufacturing know-how go straight at the watt-dollar, because the US Treasury can issue bills but not magnets.
The toll booths
On any board, some players earn by owning the squares others must cross. In 2026 the biggest toll booths are not always banks.

blocks.q: Under the GENIUS Act, what must back a compliant US stablecoin, and who earns the interest?
blocks.a: Cash, bank deposits and Treasury bills of 93 days or less. The issuer and its distribution partners earn the interest. Holders cannot be paid interest by the issuer.

blocks.q: Why does this project say energy is replacing gold's old job rather than the dollar?
blocks.a: Because delivered energy is the scarce physical limit on how much real output money can buy, as gold once was, and energy assets increasingly back dollar loans. But a kilowatt-hour is perishable, local and getting cheaper, so it fails as spendable money.

rules: New rails, old anchors. Ask what sits under any new money, and who earns the interest on it.
Gold is insurance against the system, not a tool inside it. Hold it as insurance, not as income.
Find the toll booths. The people who own the crossing points earn whether players win or lose.
